en: First Chapter:
She whose body is the sky, yet who possesses a female form— O Umā, mother of the entire world, [protect] us who are distressed by darkness and by suffering.
May he favor us with the moonlight of his smile, moistened by the nectar of compassion.

I bow to that indescribable Great Power (Mahāśakti), who flows through all things, whose waves are visible through the yoga of unconditioned awareness (nirupādhivimarśa), and who is undecaying, unborn, and immeasurable. 1.2.
In reality, she is the pervasive power of austerity belonging to the Lord of Truth everywhere;
through the body of a playful woman, she is the daughter of Himavat, the Kuṇḍalinī within embodied beings.

The Supreme Person is said to be the navel of the worlds, and the world of truth (satyaloka) is [the region] around it; the subtle power that flows forth from there is the world of austerity (tapoloka). 1.4.
The outpouring from the fire of the Supreme Person, which was like smoke rising from meanings hidden within, became the people of the world, with their powers as flames at the surrounding edges. 1.5.
The world, which is like an extremely subtle smoke, is pervaded by another name, namely *nāka* (the celestial realm).
Beyond even that, the supreme power (*parā śakti*), which is more subtle still, pervades from within.
That power which is like smoke, internal heat, and pure flame—some call it *div* (heaven), while others call it the supreme *vyoman* (ether). 1.7.
This vast and boundless world of great people, which is like a mass of rising smoke, they call by such names as *vyoman*, *antarikṣa*, and *gagana*. 1.8.

In the extremities, a certain individual soul, distinct from the Power, having become separated from the Supreme Self through association with the limiting adjunct of space, emerged as a self-conceited ego. 1.9.
This world of light is the path spoken of as being beyond perception;
the power (śakti) born from its womb, having attained her own nature therein, is called Dākṣāyaṇī.

The first manifestation of the Satyas is proclaimed as occurring even prior to [the emergence of] Śakti, through the accomplishment of a distinct sense of egoity within that which consists of the egoity of Īśa. (1.11)
Thus, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), Śakti is the mother of Ākāśa, though in reality she is his progenitor;
likewise, the Vedic scripture remains uncontradicted in stating that Dakṣa was born from Aditi and Aditi from Dakṣa.
Some scholars say that Satī and Bhava are the mother and father of the worlds; others, according to the speech of the learned, say they are Aditi and Prajāpati. (1.13)
When the Lord assumed a divine male form for the sake of sport and for his delight,
the Mother of the worlds likewise assumed the form of a divine woman.

They call her Umā, the daughter of Himavat, whose form possesses radiant golden ornaments, who is exceedingly beautiful, who is the very essence of the Lord’s delight, and whose fame is purifying. 1.15.
The first witness of his body—among those who dwell in the world and possess beautiful eyes—is the Lord of the Gods, whose vision is as clear as a pillar and who is of incomparable merit. (1.16)

I meditate upon that body of the fair-eyed Śivā, which is as soft as a young sprout, purified by the fire upon the altar, radiant with the luster of precious jewels, and as lovely as a crescent of the new moon. 1.17.
Some describe the goddess Gaurī as a woman born from the divine essence of the Snowy Mountain (Himavat), whose excellence is reckoned by those who have tasted her supreme beauty. 1.18.
Let this story be true; nevertheless, one should understand that form described by the devotees as some indescribable portion of the primordial Light.
Some think that what was called a "dense mountain" was spoken of with intentional ambiguity, since from it there arises an unbearable, deep-sounding power. (1.20)

That the sky bestows food upon the cattle by means of its own mass of dust is not celebrated as the sacrifice of Dakṣa in this world; rather, it is known as the narrative of the sacrifice of Dakṣa. (1.21)

Although it is all-pervasive, that power remains hidden and appears lost from the perspective of the observer's intellect; its cessation within that sacrificial rite is declared to be the manifestation of the Real.
If this exceedingly powerful Śakti belonging to the one named Parvata becomes manifest from the Vedic language (ghana), that is declared to be the birth of Pārvatī.
A portion of Śiva’s splendor was bestowed here upon the Himālaya for the sake of blessing those who dwell on earth;
that his presence was granted is one thing, but this other [matter] is his playful conduct.
Those who understand the meaning of these noble verses as it is agreed upon in the scriptures should recognize the Goddess Ambika as the sovereign queen of the worlds. 1.25
The Second Chapter:
Description of the Creation, etc. (In the Pañcacāmara meter) He who, with reverence, [is adorned] by a garland of white pārijāta flowers...
Adorning her throat, she speaks even without sound;
may this charming smile of Maheśa’s meritorious consort lead to my prosperity and to the dispelling of my sins. 2.1.
The body of the Lord, who possesses a male form, is a playful woman who constantly flows with the essence of compassion; she is enchanting to men,
her face radiant with a smile like waves of nectar, and she is auspicious.
May [the Lord] who rests upon his lotus feet destroy for me the fruit of my sins. || 2.2 ||
She who creates, she who sustains, and she who destroys the three worlds; she who shines everywhere and yet is not seen anywhere;
she whose form is exceedingly hidden, [remaining so] without the instruction of a Guru.
And even by the wise, the beautiful woman who creates darkness cannot be understood.
For the sake of the complete unfolding and illumination of this mass of beings— who are akin to a great darkness,
lying dormant within the abode of all seeds, sealed in silence—
there came into being [the powers].
Having performed this great deed for me, she is my chosen deity.
From the womb of Maheśa, from the seed-vessel of all beings,
she who possesses boundless divine majesty scatters the entire universe through her primordial and wondrous activity, which has shaken the sleep of the Lord.
Adored by the world, this wondrous and beginningless Power is victorious! 2.5
The Tantrikas call Him Bhava; the Vaidikas designate that Imperishable One as Sadāśiva when He is worshipped with devotion.
There is no difference in meaning between these two names; the distinction lies only in this: the first term is masculine, while the latter is neuter.
If existence is called "Bhavānī" because of its designation, O Imperishable One,
and if that which is so proclaimed is indeed You, O Mother, and if You are called "Satī," then You possess no state of being (*bhāvatā*), for You exist as the very form of power (*śakti*).
I do not understand, Kālikā, how you are distinguished from both the existent and the non-existent. || 2.7 ||
O Mother, praised by gods and asuras in the past for the work of creating the world, you are the life-force for those who proclaim existence as rooted in non-existence;
you are the intellect free from conceptual construction for those who proclaim awakening as the root.
For those who maintain that joy is the root [of liberation], the supreme flavor is independent. || 2.8 ||
Because she exists as such, she is Bhavānī; she is beginningless and devoid of end.
She eternally pervades the worlds, and because she has arisen from him (Bhava), she is Umā.
She is perceived by all as being of the nature of aesthetic essence (rasa); therefore, she is called Śivā.
Thus, the wise declare that the consciousness of the Lord is threefold. || 2.9 ||
The supreme consciousness itself, when joined with some aesthetic flavor (rasa), is desire; the supreme consciousness itself is always the activity of the Indestructible;
and the supreme consciousness itself is known as the intellect (mati) that illumines objects of perception.
Thus, the ancient authorities declare that consciousness is threefold, or otherwise. || 2.10 ||
O Mother, while the Lord desires to act, this expanse of the sky is overspread by a mass of smoke scattered from the series of your blazing stakes;
you who were formerly the very form of Śiva’s sovereignty through his creative emission, you are now perceived as a distinct sovereign in Puṣkara.

Furthermore, O Mother Umā, who consists of the vision of Maheśa, in former times you fashioned spheres of light from the minute particles of the sky—dense with the maturation [of karma] and appearing here and there as objects of the eye, blazing intensely like the mass of roots of ten million cosmic eggs and trees. (2.12)
Within the lattice of smoke from the fire of austerity, there arise fiery atoms,
vital atoms, and earthly atoms;
such is the gradual emission [of these] through the majesty of the ripening of the Lord’s power.
Let the orb of the thousand-rayed sun, its range of perception and so forth, be grasped.
O Mother, having placed Your foot upon the circle of the Sun, the garlanded with rays, as You strove through Your form of the power of light,
this earth was fashioned together with the planets, beginning with Maṅgala, by means of the three-fold atomic particles gathered from the treasury of the sky.
O Goddess, even with such extensive dismissal, you remained unsatisfied; therefore, you have once again performed this extraordinary act.
O Mother, in this interval between the earth and the orb of the sun, the fruit of this deed is the lunar disc.
O Śivā, you and Īśvara have both assumed the forms of a bride and a groom here in this world in order to sport playfully;
oh Kālī, those who speak of wonders say that the Lord, whose body is the sky, is born from your womb as your son.
Furthermore, that golden person within the sun is not perceived by the mind alone, nor merely by his golden form;
rather, O Mother, this other form of the Lord, which consists of his effects, is said by the wise to be his body reflected here within the hearts of men.
And you yourself, with a body radiant like gold, are present within the sun, O Prabhākara; and you are reflected within him among men.
O Goddess, you are the deity of aesthetic flavor (rasa) in the lotus and in the sun.
You are the deity of the rays; you are the deity of enjoyment among embodied beings.
O Ambikā, having repeatedly sent forth many embodied beings here upon the earth and there into the sun in the sky, you two,
O Imperishable Ones, have gone to guide the ancestors who have become moons of the earth.
And there, O Queen of the Manifestation, you two assumed slender forms through your illusory power.
In the midst of the sky, they proclaim the all-pervading Hara to be golden;
they say the lotus-seated Brahmā is reflected in the orb of the sun;
and here within our own inner self, they speak of Viṣṇu, the infallible Acyuta.
This Sāvitrī is the lineage of those who proclaim the threefold nature of all living beings.
Within the midst of the sky, they declare the Lord to have a golden body, the Person within the solar orb known by the name Hiraṇyagarbha;
He shines as the imperishable Virāj within the Virāj for the sake of men.
But this conceptualization of names belongs only to those who know the reality of Sāvitrī.
O Mother, they say that in the sky there is Soma with a golden body,
and within the orb of the sun is Purandara reflected;
and here within the interior of embodied beings, they speak of the radiant Agni.
This is the traditional method [of interpretation] for those who perceive the words of the ancient sages regarding Śiva. || 2.22 ||

O Śivā, for those who propound the fivefold forms, the two [forms] as charming as the speech-bride of the lotus-eyed one are as before; the person within the lunar orb is named Rudra; the golden one born in the intermediate space is Īśvara; and Sadāśiva is the eternal reality, O lady of golden limbs. (2.23)
Then, from the Lord, Pramā was born; thereafter, she herself,

possessing a body, appeared separately in the sky as Pramāvatī, while the Lord remained there in his golden form with the appearance of a golden woman, and [another] in the midst of the sky within the sun.
Likewise, in the intermediate spaces between the bodies of embodied beings, the Great Goddess Umā is victorious.
May my Mother, whose lotus feet are far removed from the reach of the wicked-minded, destroy the thicket of suffering for the entire world;
and may these five chowries, resting upon priceless cushions, attain the form of her anklets with their delicate steps.
The Third Chapter:
The Means for [Attaining] Her Embodied State (composed in the *tanumadhyā* meter).
May even a mere fragment of the Mother’s bright smile, [brought] by the wind, [protect] us.
May he bring an end to the inner darknesses. 3.1.
They are the first parents of the worlds; they are irreproachable and worthy of worship by gods, asuras, and mortals alike. (3.2)
One says that those two [the moon and sun] are distinct when they possess physical forms; another poet says that the *dvandva* compound denotes a single body. (3.3)
Another, filled with doubt, speaks of Śakti as being devoid of body and Īśa as being the male, regarding the woman. (3.4)
Some desire that very Lord as pure existence alone; others sing of Brahman as one, without Śakti. (3.5)
Some know the Lord as being devoid of body yet endowed with wisdom;
they know His power to be unimpeded wisdom.
While some maintain what has been said [by others], others say again:
"The binding of the Lord's illusory body is not due to power. (3.7)
Nature declares that those whose parents are both still embodied, or even one of them, [must be honored]. (3.8)
That those two, mother and father, are one body is some kind of play for the purpose of manifesting variety. 3.9.
In the case of effects such as human beings, there would be an expansion of the intellect and the mind that is devoid of a cause, [if they were] merely talk about existence. (3.10)
The Advaitins must resort to some other form of *māyā*; is that [power] something distinct from *śakti*, or what is the use of further arguments? 3.11.
The self would not be distinct from its power; what then [is the role] of the limiting adjunct?
Or rather, it is the mind resting in the eye that possesses the form of the universe. (3.12)
If those two [atoms] were exclusively devoid of extension and extremely subtle, they would have to be described as incapable of assuming the form of a body for playful sport. (3.13)
Bestowing grace upon his devotees through divine and wondrous play, the manifestation of that form should be understood as possessing a radiant meaning. 3.14
If femininity is not desired, why is masculinity desired? Or rather, would it not be inferable that there is no woman at all? (3.15)
Therefore, those two wise parents should be addressed,
who, though subtle, have once again assumed bodies for their divine play.
The two forms of Śakti and Īśvara do not conform to our [limited] bodies;
one is of the nature of nectar, while the other is the essence of the Praṇava.
Producing a divine, dense radiance and accompanied by sound, the form whose essence is the *praṇava* perceives everything without exception. 3.18.
Divine, with thick soma and flowing essence, he enjoys the multitude of worlds as his body of nectar. 3.19
Awakening without support is indeed the divine fire;
pure joy is indeed the divine moon. (3.20)
By the power of the resolve of his parents and of the worlds, he attained the state of density as both the moon and the sun. (3.21)
O Goddess, you worship that Lord whose body consists of consciousness; indeed, you are one whose limbs are composed of bliss. 3.22
Divine is your body, divine are your garments;
O Mother, divine are your golden ornaments.
O Goddess, that which is seen as your face is not an ordinary body;
this is your Māyā, which transcends all logical reasoning.
May these modern women of slender waist rightly propagate this ancient woman of slender waist among the assemblies of the learned. 3.25.
The Fourth Chapter:
Internal Splendors (in the Gīti meter) Emerging once more from the essence of the moon’s orb, it is exceedingly subtle.
May that gentle smile from the face of Gaurī, which is the very essence [of beauty], remove the web of our suffering. 4.1.
O Queen of Mṛtyuñjaya, you are victorious—you who breathe within the *kulakuṇḍa*, who are conscious within the hearts of all living beings, and who contemplate [him] at the crown of the head. 4.2.

O Mother, through the essences of fire, water, and food, three subtle atoms (aṇus) are formed at the root, the heart, and the head; from their digestion, there arise for embodied beings [the powers] that pervade the three worlds.

O you of immeasurable power, when the craftsmanship of the body is complete, having gone through the gateway known as the *brahmarandhra* by way of the channel-path, you shall enter the radiant, subtle atom.
Having first entered by means of a portion, you go forth again from that;
you emerge through two paths, the veins established as being both behind and in front.
O Mother, in that state of coming and going, your skeletal frame exists as a limitation, extending from the crown of your head down to the root-base (mūlādhāra). 4.6.
O Mother of the World, those who delight in indirect speech call you Kuṇḍalinī because of your resemblance to the form of a lute as you sport among human bodies. (4.7)
For that adept who constantly perceives the power within this body as flowing from the cranial aperture of the sky, there is no need for any other yogic practices. 4.8.
O Mother of the worlds, you enter all beings equally and you emerge from them equally;
if you are known, it leads to power, but if you are not known, it leads to egoism.
If descent is meditated upon, the ascent of power will be marvelous;
in that state, this body becomes like a great machine of lightning-fire. (4.10)
For those who ascend [the stages], there is the production of mere egoity within the heart;
thereafter, this body exists for pleasure or pain according to experience. (4.11)

O Mother, that individuality which belongs to living beings—the ego-sense and the ground of all notions of difference—is, for You, that very Being itself appearing as if distinct due to its reliance upon limiting adjuncts. 4.12
They call this ignorance the seed of the great tree of saṃsāra, O Goddess, which is endowed with all juices and fruits and is nourished by the water of prārabdha karma. 4.13
O Mother, in the low-lying body that bestows individuality, your power flows incessantly like a canal for all living beings, manifesting wondrous forms, O Goddess. (4.14)
The wise know this mind, which is the subtle essence residing in the heart;
some call it the supreme vital breath (prāṇa), the root of the five winds. 4.15

For those who employ the term "mind" (citta) as a synonym for "intellect" (manas) and are ignorant of their distinction, worldly discourse depends upon that [intellect]; however, the cognition of reality is otherwise. 4.16.
O Goddess, from that unstruck [sound] shining to the right, within the cave named Dahara,
some indescribable ray of light (raśmikalā) bestows grace upon the mind from the Kula-vessel.
O Śivā, your mind, though subtle and appearing as a mere fraction the size of a thumb, becomes like a stainless mirror that draws forth the reflection of Brahman. 4.18

They say that this reflection of the Lord, which resembles a whirlpool and is bodiless, appears like a thumb in size when measured by the light of the mental states associated with limiting adjuncts. 4.19.
O Śivā, the reflections of the forms of the couple appear in the eyes; yet in the heart, which is the primordial womb (kulakuṇḍa), there is a certain radiance of those who are indeed formless. 4.20.
He who knows that the jewel of the mind is his wealth—worth more than any worldly price—and that it is deposited within the cave of the heart, abandons all external hopes. (4.21)

Not yet having reached the summit, but having set out from the heart and being sustained by the channel, your radiant intellect has been spoken of; O Goddess, that steadfastness in you becomes the ultimate steadfastness.

O Maheśvarī, the light of the intellect that has reached the atom consisting of food (annamaya-aṇu)—a radiance like that of the moon or the sun—is designated as "mind" (manas), the locus where volition (saṅkalpa) arises. 4.23.
O beloved of Maheśa, that person who worships you—the power of consciousness flashing within the mind at every single thought—attains your feet. 4.24
May these songs attend upon the beloved of the Lord of the Universe, who has abandoned sleep and is moving about here on the bed of the *ādhāra-cakra*. 4.25.
The wedding procession (composed in the upajāti meter): Repeatedly applying, as it were, a coating of sandalwood paste to the cheeks of their friends.
May the glorious splendors of the sprouts of the smile from the beloved of Śrīkaṇṭha illuminate the worlds. || 5.1 ||

May the white fame of the flower-armed god, elevated by his victory over the golden mountain-bow, and the beauty of the gentle smile of the mother of the elephant-faced one, extend to you most abundant prosperity. 5.2.
May the slight fragments of the playful smile of the Mother of Vighneśa—resembling pure, clear, falling snow, rising from the waves of the mass of nectar being churned—make your desire fruitful. 5.3.
May this certain moonlight, serene and satisfying as it becomes the guest of Maheśa’s eye,
bring fulfillment to our heart's desire.
The radiance of a fragment of Maheśvarī’s smile. || 5.4 ||

May those who sport with the moving hem of the garment upon their white breasts, whose splendor is like the laughter of the consort of the enemy of the three cities, utterly dispel our misfortunes. 5.5.

May those smiles of the deer-eyed consort of the Lord of Beings bring us relief from fatigue—smiles whose radiance bears the grace of camphor powder upon the cheeks of the young women of the quarters. 5.6.
Let those smiles of the Daughter of the Mountain of your lineage bear fruit as they wish—those smiles by whose rays a new spring is created within the garden groves of the White Mountain. (5.7)
The splendor of the smiles of Śiva’s consort is a reduplication of the luster of her ornaments’ moonlight, and a twofold repetition of the brilliance of her nose-ornaments. It is my [sole] delight.
May they fulfill all our desires. || 5.8 ||

O Mother, having fashioned the abode of the universe together with you, the expert in the arts, Śarva—that artisan—desiring to sport, wished to take you as his wife, you who had become a woman, while he himself became a man. (5.9)
Wearing a divine, white silk garment,
shining with a braid of hair resembling the lord of serpents,
you possess eyes like blossoming lotuses.
You have stolen away the eyes of the Lord of Proliferation.
That supreme, blazing ornament binding his limbs, which resembled the coils of the king of serpents,
gratified the eyes of the Sustainer of the Universe, who is solely intent upon the Self.
You were the source of joy for the first Manu, and he too became the object of your affection;
O Mother, that was not only the seed of the bond of matrimony between you two, but of the entire institution of marriage as well.
The conduct of your policy, exceedingly beautiful, and the laughter of Śiva, which steals the splendor of the new moon—
both of these performed the preliminary rites for the festival of the wedding of Ādirāma.
O Thou who art praised by all, may You— able to give, capable of consoling, competent to act, and powerful to rebuke— protect me.
But his hand was grasped by the bearer of the cool-rayed moon.
O Supreme One, you cannot be touched by others; he cannot be conceived by another.
You alone belong to Śarva, and he alone belongs to you, O Mother.
Thus, let this marital union of yours be true.

Having produced another moon from the moon upon his own crest, Śambhu gave it to you as a crest-ornament; O lady of auspicious limbs, having reached your braid of hair, it shone like the night personified.
When you were born in the house of the lord of elephants,
that Lord dwelt there,
O Goddess, beholding you like lightning.
The loveliness of the puppet. || 5.17 ||
He has set out to accomplish that which is already accomplished;
and Madana was consumed in a single kalpa while practicing yoga,
so as to bear the fame of his lord, Giriśa, as "the Subduer."
And for you, however, [he gave her] Aparṇā, in order to establish his fame. || 5.18 ||
If even you have performed such terrible austerity for the sake of bestowing grace upon the former form of your husband,
O Mother of All, who here would abandon effort?
May a living being attain even that goal which is connected [to the truth]. 5.19.
With his matted locks aflame, a mark of fire upon his forehead, wearing a garland of skulls and an elephant hide as his garment,
adorned with serpents and having ashes for his bodily unguent.
The enemy of flowers, with a harsh, loud laugh. || 5.20 ||
O sinless-limbed one, if a man dwelling in the cremation ground and bearing a trident has stolen your heart,
this matter has not even reached the stage of being an illustration.
"Affection depends upon external causes. (5.21)
This form belongs to Purāri, or rather, it is that very same; and this activity is [the same] as in other times.
Yet he assumes this lovely body and these even lovelier gestures in order to sport with you.
With the yakṣas rejoicing, the siddhas assembled, the lord of the gaṇas dancing, and the lord of the munis blossoming with joy,
may there be union for you two once again on the Himālaya.
He bore the peerless greatness of his mother. || 5.23 ||
O lady of faultless limbs, Maheśvara, having married you, obtained two preeminent sons;
of these two, one wanders about seeking to devour the universe.
Alas, another takes refuge on the slopes of the mountains! || 5.24 ||
Proclaiming the auspicious tidings of the Mother of the worlds, whose fame is most lovely,
may these [verses] bring joy to the virtuous.
For us, the *upajāti* meters are pure in their structural composition. 5.25.
May those who steal the fame of the moon, who create fresh splendors, and who are the husbands of the mother of Skanda— the sweet smiles— possess great fortune for me. (In the Madalekhā meter) 6.1.
May the slight smiles of my mother, which bring an exceedingly brilliant abundance of flowers to the creepers of the quarters, lead to your prosperity. 6.2.
O beloved of Bharga, if even a single smile of yours were capable of bringing about the manifestation of the universe, what further hymn could there be for you? 6.3
O Kālī, when you were sporting in the garden called Viyat, how could my meager speech measure you, who were like a ball made of globes? 6.4.
The sky is your pleasure palace; what office is this?
O Mother, this earth, abundant with food, is your dining hall.
You are the giver of intellects, you are the leader of accomplishments;
you are the casket of heroic powers, you are the assault upon all tasks. 6.6
You are the essence of the sciences, you are the charm of the heart;
you are the play of the gods, you are the sport of the Daityas.
You are the activity of all that moves, and you are the stability of all that is stationary;
you are the root of the worlds, and you are the net from which the worlds arise.
In the investigation of the principles (tattva), the Goddess is the all-pervading power of light;
in the investigation of her form, she is a woman exceedingly delicate. (6.9)
Where is this great light, more vast even than space? And where is that slender-limbed woman who subdues it all? 6.10
He gave sovereignty to the Lord of the Gods, a thousand rays to the Sun,
heat to Fire, and moonlight to the King of Herbs.
He offered his immeasurable vigor to Vāyu, his vastness to Ākāśa,
his solidity to Vasudhā, and his state of fluidity to Toya.
The great fortune of the gods exceeds ten million;
the various supernatural powers of men exceed a hundred thousand. (6.13)
O Goddess, bestowing the power of stability upon stationary things and the power of motion upon moving things from some internal treasury of Your own, You alone grant these gifts.
Producing wonder and sustaining every object—alas, O my mother, you are some woman of delicate limbs! 6.15
In this woman with limbs so supple that she bends under the weight of her hips—if such power exists here, is it not surely illusion? (6.16)
Your form is slender-limbed, your speech has a soft resonance;
your bow is the sweet sugarcane, and your hand is most delicate.
Your pair of eyes is tremulous, and timidity is manifest in you; who here would believe that the entire universe is under your control? 6.18.
O charming Gaurī, if you knit your brows upon your lotus-face,
even the elemental spirits will tremble with fear and the stars themselves will be made to quiver.
O Sovereign Lady of the Inner Chambers, if there is any desire of Śambhu’s,
then even a terrible fire may become cool, and from within a mass of grass, a most fearsome fire may emerge.
To behold the boundless universe is the burden of your beloved;
to accomplish every task is the burden of you, O illustrious Mother.
O Mother, you alone are the Lord who has visibly assumed the vow; you are the sole witness capable of creating, sustaining, or indeed destroying everything.
O Mother, honored by the gods, I believe that you are always like a child when you repeatedly destroy these cosmic eggs. 6.23
O Rāma, who has revived Kāma through your divine play and who is devoted to Śaṅkara,
make me, your devotee, capable and intent upon the worship of your feet.
O Consort of the Lord of All, may these Madalekhās of Hairaṃbha, possessing purifying fragrances, bring you satisfaction. 6.25.
She whose body is the sky, and whose manifestations are the Mātṛkās and other powers—
she who is like a royal swan for the lotus-eye of Speech,
having emerged from the abode of her lotus-face.
May the gentle smile of Harasundarī, which appears during conversation with those standing here, bring us exceeding well-being. 7.1.
You are the primordial sound (*nāda*), you are speech, you are radiance, and you are the indivisible consciousness;
though consciousness appears fragmented, it remains the undivided essence, O Beloved of the Lord of all!
O Sovereign, you are the collective totality of all powers (*nikhila-śakti-samasthi*).
I bow to you, whose body is fashioned from the intermediate space. || 7.2 ||
Those thousands of powers that shine forth, whose majesty is renowned throughout the three worlds,
are the collective totality of which this [deity] is seen as a most wondrous treasury.
O Sovereign of the World, you are the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the universe.

O Mother of the World, destroyer of the sorrow of those who take refuge in you, that which is imagined by the power of the mind as some form of yours is not truly known; yet it is the very body thus imagined that destroys grief.
Your name, whose abode is beyond words, is being inscribed.
Let those skilled in the ancient lore speak of you as a woman endowed with a physical form, O Mother of all the worlds;
let that be true, for it is but some playful manifestation (*līlā*) of yours, while your actual body is the divine *rajas*.

O Giver of Boons, that mass of dust which, though its pure form is not defiled by the dust of earthly birth, exists as some indescribable cloud of particles in the vast expanse of space— that is Your body, O Great One, both exceedingly vast and yet most subtle.
The wise call that alone the path of the gods. || 7.6 ||
O Goddess, you who are the refuge of the gods, who are difficult for those submerged in worldly existence to reach,
and who are called Vairocanī, blazing with ascetic fervor; you whose body is anointed with the splendor of the Sun, the friend of the lotus.
That body of yours becomes worthy of praise by all the gods with beautiful joints.
Your vital breaths shine here, and your heart shines here; here are your eyes by the hundreds, and here are your ears;
here are your olfactory organs, as well as your tongues and your skins.
O Goddess, here are the feet of speech, and here are the hands.
O Mother, you see everywhere and hear from all sides;
you eat and smell everywhere,
and you touch everything at all times without distinction.
O Goddess, who would be able to describe your good fortune?

O Mother, you rejoice everywhere, you release yourself on all sides; O Goddess, you wander everywhere and roar from every direction. O Sovereign, who is capable of defining the wondrous variety of the web of your actions? 7.10
O Mother of the Universe, how many lords of light are there in you?
How many lands are there, encompassed by oceans of various kinds?
And how many orbs are there of the shining cool-rayed moon?
And no wise man, however learned, knows this.
O Goddess, praised in all the Agamas, you pervade the entire atmosphere with a portion of the unmanifest sound;
through the influence of limiting adjuncts, you are both this primordial resonance (nāda) and the words of speech.
The wise call you Brāhmī, possessing such immeasurable glory.

O Mother of the multitude of worlds, you manifest all things clearly through various forms that are waves of the one, partless, profound, and great Light; O You of uncontracted power, this is indeed declared by the lords of sages to be your Vaiṣṇavī energy.
O Mother, you place your individuality within every heart, whereby the inner self seems both shattered and yet bound;
this very art of yours is the mistress of the thread for the drama of the world.
Thus has been described your conscious majesty as Māheśvarī.

That which manifests as the illuminator of the stainless reality within the lotus of the heart— fully blossomed, possessing a perfectly pure being through the power of purity of sustenance, and maintaining constant and stable mindfulness— is [the wisdom of the Tathāgata].
As such, O Savitrī, you are remembered as the power (śakti) of Guru Guha.

By whom the dwellers of heaven receive the sweet oblation (*havya*), by whom the ancestors partake of the delightful ancestral offering (*kavya*), and by whom every person indeed eats their food; The final line of the verse is: *saivādyatve 'pi ca vidhau parikalpyate naḥ* (That very same [power] is conceived by us even now in the ritual procedure. (Note: The provided text fragment ends with "yayaiva", which is the relative pronoun *yayā* in the instrumental case, feminine singular, agreeing with the implied subject *śaktiḥ* or *māyā*).
"O Mother, that art of yours which has the face of a boar is sung [in the scriptures]. 7.16.

O Goddess, you slay the wicked directly for the protection of the worlds, and you cause them to be slain by others who are great and of proven strength; since the power of the enemy of Bala (Indra) has its strength tested by the maneuvers of the thunderbolt, this is declared to be your own sovereign majesty.

O Goddess, by Your power— which increases through the drinking of the blood of the ear-rings of *saṅkalpa* (mental constructs)— and by Your majesty, which pierces the armor of the moon-heads of the fierce fire at the root (*mūlāgni*) during the practice of the yoga of waking and deep meditation;
O Goddess, what could not have been accomplished by Cāmuṇḍā with her bodies? || 7.18 ||
O Queen of the World, you are Mūlamāyā in the Supreme Self;
Jālamāyā in Śakra, the lord of all the gods;
and Yogamāyā in the Inner Person, the Lord of Shadows.
To those whose hearts are attached to saṃsāra, you are the illusion of the snare.
You are the sleep of experience (anubhūti-nidrā) in Śiva, the sustainer of beings;
you are the sleep of delight (moda-nidrā) in Indra, the drinker of Soma;
and you are the yogic sleep (yoga-nidrā) in Viṣṇu, whose self is the orb of the seven-horsed sun.
You are the sleep of delusion for those whose hearts are submerged in saṃsāra.

O Mother, Bhuvaneśvarī, that fierce Kālī— resplendent with a body possessing a luster like thick collyrium— who was praised by Viṣṇu when he was released from the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha while seated upon the thousand-petaled lotus, is surely some portion of You.

O Mother, that form of yours which consists of the radiance of lightning—most invincible to enemies, fiercely powerful, and capable of effecting the destruction of all—is such that by meditating upon it here, a man has no fear of sin. (7.22)
O Maheśvarī, she who rendered Śumbha and Niśumbha— the world’s sole heroes— into ashes upon the tips of her tridents,
that Kauśikī of illustrious fame and slender waist is some portion of yourself, born from your own body.
O Māyā, O Śivā, O Mother who destroys the calamities of those who have sought refuge in you, look upon me with a gaze cooled by the weight of your grace;
here I am, accompanied by my son, wife, and friends.
O Goddess, I have gone for refuge to your feet. 7.24
May these *vasantatilaka* verses of the elephant among poets, composed with tender words, delight the heart of the beloved of Śiva;
and may they gladden the assembly of virtuous men who take refuge in them, dispelling all suffering and accomplishing every desired aim. (7.25)
The Threefold Conduct (in Anuṣṭubh meter):
May the destroyer of darkness on all sides, the daybreak for the smile of Caṇḍikā, be prepared to cause the lotuses of the hearts of the virtuous to blossom. 8.1.
O friend, that sleep which belongs to all beings, and which is the yogic sleep of the Lord of Ramā— let that Mahākālī, the companion of Mahākāla, be praised.
O Mother Kālī, if you do not release [him] when praised by Viriñca, how can Acyuta effect the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha? (8.3)
Vāsava, who adorned the quarters of the sky with his fame that shone like the Kāśa flower, turned his back in battle because of [the king's] exceedingly fierce prowess. (8.4)
Scorched by his majesty, I believe that even today the divine Fire-god, bearing the form of the submarine fire (*bāḍaba*), does not abandon his dwelling in the ocean. (8.5)
While he was engaged in the slaughter of living beings, Antaka’s mind was struck with wonder, and his thought was: "He alone is Death; it is not I. (8.6)
Because he disregarded and abandoned the Rākṣasa in battle,
Koṇeśa has long since attained glory among the lords of the quarters, beginning with Hari.
The fame of the Restrainer became tarnished because he was unable to restrain those wicked deeds performed by the wicked. (8.8)
Defeated by the prowess of his arms, the Wind-god for the most part became the servant of his pleasure at the end of the nights, when the amorous dalliance was over. (8.9)
Having abandoned his treasures and fled, the king of kings clearly demonstrated that life is sweeter than everything else. (8.10)
In which [kingdom], the eleven lords of the northeast became blunted, their fame reduced to that of their own throats. (8.11)
He, who considered himself a hero, felt ashamed after having conquered the moon— which had already been surpassed by the very faces of his own wives in their inner apartments.
As he played with his heroic companions like a child with toys, the sun, garlanded with rays, became for him a mere play-ball. (8.13)
The Sudarśana discus of Viṣṇu, which wards off the playful movements of the brows of the women of the inner apartments of the three cities, could find no opening against him.
Salutations again and again to that Caṇḍikā, born from the bodies of all the gods, who slew that Dānava of great prowess, Mahiṣa.

O Lord who rides upon the lion, by meditating incessantly upon your face— which is so captivating that one can never look away— Mṛḍa himself has, in the course of time, attained the very form of your countenance.

Victorious is the auspicious Śivā, whose face is like the moon of the month of Kārtika, whose creeper-like arms are the waves of the Yamunā, whose feet are like red lotuses, and who possesses the threefold radiance.

That your mass of hair is black and that your arm is the protector of the world—both these are fitting for you, O Śivā; yet it is improper that your waist is unadorned, for you are not the Queen of Heaven.
From his own body, a goddess emerged like a lamp from a lamp,
appearing to remove the calamities of the gods who were offering praise.
The gods and asuras regarded her as a jewel among womankind, endowed as she was with fortitude, cleverness, profundity, heroism, and beauty. (8.20)
Dhūmrākṣa became an oblation in the fire of his *huṃ*-utterance before he could even reach the conclusion of his boastful threats.
In that age of terrible prowess, Cāmuṇḍā and Śivadūtī devoured the forms of the Rākṣasas along with their reputations. (8.22)
I bow to that Umā, named Kauśikī, whose fame eclipsed the glory of Śumbha and Niśumbha upon the stake, and who is possessed of stainless renown.
I bow to that divine Nandā, the mother of Yaśodā from whose womb she was born, who is the glory of Gokula and dwells upon the Vindhya mountains. 8.24
Let these women, adorned with beautiful ornaments and possessing eyes like perfected lotuses, worship Ambikā while reciting the Caṇḍī-anuṣṭubh verses, as if they were themselves personified success.
A gentle smile (in the Āryā metre):
May the blossoming of the face of Śiva’s consort, which teaches us the purity of the moonlight of the bright fortnight of autumn, remain awake for our protection. 9.1.
May the gracious countenance of Gaurī grant us clarity of heart—a countenance that is a commentary on joy and a rejection of the autumnal moon. 9.2.
May the laughter of the deer-eyed consort of Hara—like a certain wave from the internal ocean of the milk of joy—render my mind free from all impurity. 9.3

May the laughter of the Mistress of the Heart of Paśupati bestow auspiciousness upon us—laughter that quenches the heat of the biting stings spreading in every direction and dispels all impurity. 9.4.
May the smiles of the beautiful-eyed consort of Giriśa, which dispel the inner darkness and mock the beloved of Rohiṇī, serve for my awakening. 9.5.
Wandering upon the stage of the sky together with the rays of the moonlight of his speech, may the laughter of the belly of the consort of the Destroyer of Cities take away my sin. 9.6.
May the smiles from the side-glances of Rudrāṇī destroy our misfortunes—those smiles whose rising is the very day for the moon, the nectar-rayed ornament [of her face]. 9.7.

May the moonlight of the gentle smile from the moon-like face of the Mother of the Skandhas nourish us—she upon whom depends the narrative that brings joy to the night-lotuses of the sages' minds. 9.8.
May that moonlight known as Gaurī’s gentle smile grant us our desires—she whose companion is the star-like pearl of the lovely garland around her neck. 9.9.
May the smile of the beloved of Hara, which dwells together with the mass of rays from the pearl necklaces upon his faultless throat, remove all my ignorance. 9.10
Like a fish [in the water], may the smile of the daughter of the Lord of Ilādhara—which is the supreme object of both knowledge and perception—fulfill every desire of our minds. 9.11.
May that smile of Śivā protect us—she who, though small in size, performed no small deed by merely casting a glance upon Śaṅkara and making him the servant of her peerless arrows. 9.12.

May he who, through his skill in the application of aesthetic emotion, causes even Śiva—who is beyond the reach of passion—to experience love for Smarā (Pārvatī), and who is honored by the assembly of the twice-born, protect us as the proclaimer of Śiva’s laughter. 9.13.
May the laughter of Pārvatī, the charioteer of the five-arrowed god who desires to conquer the fire-eyed one, protect me with her arrows while she wears red garments. 9.14.
May that smile of the pearl from the lineage of the Lord of Mountains—which pierces the vital points of Śiva’s heart and whose splendor is doubled by the luster of her teeth—dispel my sorrow. 9.15.
May the smile—the auspicious ointment for the face—of the actress who plays upon the stage of the universe and is the companion of Śiva, the stage-manager, purify us. 9.16.
May the youthful lover of the consort of Hara, who delights upon a bed of fresh coral shoots and is graced by the playful radiance of his nose-ornament, take away our sorrow. 9.17.

May the child-like laughter of the Daughter of the Mountain protect our entire lineage, as it plays together with the fawns that are the rays of her nose-ornament upon the altar of her lower lip. 9.18.

May the laughter of the sovereign mistress of Śiva’s life—manifesting as a doubling of the ointment upon her breasts and a parting of the silken garment on her slopes—remove the anguish of my heart. 9.19.
May the playful smile of Girijā, which respectfully welcomes with words of greeting the ash that serves as the body-unguent of Giriśa, bestow upon me profound wisdom. 9.20.
May the smile of the Daughter of the Mountain protect me— a smile that is a lazy bubble of nectar-like speech as she converses with her beloved, who wears the young moon as his crest-jewel.
May the languid smile protect me— pure even compared to the pearl necklace resting upon the mountain-like breasts of Śiva’s consort, shining within the palace of her face’s splendor.
When the mango tree had become useless, when the blue lotus had suffered humiliation, when the ashoka had failed to attain its success, and even when the lotus had lost its glory of victory; (9.23)
May that smile of Umā, which pierced the heart of Hara in many ways with its arrow-like beauty—like a jasmine blossom—be for my prosperity. 9.24.
These noble ladies, all of whom are auspicious and marked by smiles as pure as the *amalaka* fruit, shall attend upon the goddess Umā, who is most desirable and has no equal. 9.25.
Description from Hair to Feet (in the Lalitā metre):
May the pure smiles slowly emerging from the mouth of Kātyāyanī for the cleansing of the quarters, for the prosperity of the three worlds, and for the delight of Dhūrjaṭi, protect us. 10.1.
Though very small, he spreads his rays in all directions;
though mild, he bestows pure awakening upon the virtuous; and though white, he causes passion to fade in the enemy of the Bodiless One (Śiva).
May the smile of the ancient, beautiful-eyed one purify us. || 10.2 ||
Even that which is captivating to the heart would become utterly loathsome without that which is a portion of life;
how can that infinite beauty be described?
She is the ocean of nectar and the beautiful consort of the Lord of All.
We are unable to compare her even with the wives of minor deities by means of earthly standards;
how much less, then, can we compare Umā, whose bodily radiance eclipses the eyes of the world, with all the beauties of the gods? (10.4)
The density of the mass of monsoon clouds, the rise and fall of the waves of the son of the Sun (the ocean),
and the length of the lord of serpents, Kāla— the three belong to you.
In the hair, O Goddess of the Abode of Bharga, is the triad. 10.5.

O Īśānasundarī, who in this world would not proclaim the orb of the nectar-rayed moon to be a mere lump of clay when it is so utterly inferior to the circle of your face? For in this world, nothing is more base than the mouth of a mortal woman.
The lotuses from the ponds situated in the immortal realm bring tribute for your face;
otherwise, O lady of broad locks, how could such great fragrance exist in your mouth, which is distinct from flowers?
O Sovereign of the World, may your mind take delight in the auspicious fragrance of the lotuses in the waters of the river of the realm of the gods,
even as it does in the fragrance of your own face.
But there was a surge of joy in the mind of the sovereign of the world. || 10.8 ||
O Mother, who can describe your beauty, of which even a mere fragment of the white radiance of your smile exists,
and whose bodily splendor consists of waves from the ocean?
The regions of blazing light were like creeping vines of lightning. || 10.9 ||
O Mother of the World, who does not shine before you,
the treasury of radiant smiles? Yet those very same beings, by that [smile], were rendered pale behind you.
Indeed, there might be some stroke of darkness among these. || 10.10 ||

Is it the luster of a row of teeth on your face, or the blossoming of your excellent intellect? Is it a wave of joy, or perhaps the very essence of Śaṅkara’s love for you, O Goddess—what indeed is this smile of yours? 10.11
O beloved of the Three-eyed One, with that eye of yours which spreads a mass of light across the quarters and possesses a splendor divided by ten million suns;
What is the simile for the lotus? A wise person [is the answer]. || 10.12 ||
O Śrīkarṇa, awakened by the grace of the beloved Compassion shining in the corner of your eye,
O Savitrī, [listen to] this certain hymn of mine.
Having heard it, may he extend the glory of the lineage of Bharata. || 10.13 ||
The nose of those who are engaged in meditation becomes a stabilizer for their flickering eyes;
so too is your nose a stabilizer for the eyes of the Destroyer of Cities.
O Mother, she becomes a wonderful stabilizer.

O daughter of the lineage, you surpass [the moon] in excellence by being filled with the essence of nectar, even more so than the bimba fruit, coral, or fresh sprouts; you are one who delights the mind of Śiva.
Even one who is the lowest of the low is most excellent to you.

O lady of auspicious conduct, those two breasts of yours, possessing the luster of lightning and soft like a garland of mandāra flowers that dispel heat, became the cause of bondage for Dhūrjaṭi, who is otherwise the subduer of all bonds. (10.16)
O Mother, it is truly marvelous that Dhūrjaṭi grasps these two lotus-hands of yours with such tenderness, yet they possess a most extraordinary firmness.
In whom the pride of Śumbha and others was destroyed. || 10.17 ||
O Mother of the world, may those thousands of sinless ones who drink from the fountain of nectar that is your breast reign supreme;
among them, one is the fortunate elephant-faced one.
Whom they sing of as having hands that grant everything.
O Mother of stainless virtue, your line of body hair is the noose extended from your gentle heart, cast out to lead my gaze back to the shore after it has fallen into the well of your Lord’s navel.
If you were merely the intermediate world of the sky, O fair one, those who know of your divine majesty would not be struck with wonder;
for the wise proclaim you, embodied as the enemy of the three cities, to be the three worlds themselves.

O Mother, has the flood of your ocean-like emotion, having flowed from the heart through the navel, fallen again after being split in two by the fracture of the stone of the hips; or does it flow under the guise of your lovely pair of thighs, equal to the trunks of elephants? 10.21.
O Great Mistress, O fountain of loveliness, O Creator of the world, your pair of shanks is like the twin quivers of the Lord of Rati,
enriched with arrows of secret, radiant splendor flashing within.
O Queen of the night, who governs the one whose weapon is the flower, your power causes the wicked ones residing in the three worlds to tremble;
yet, it is said, you feel fatigue in walking due to the weight of your hips.
Tell me, by what means do you attain that reality? || 10.23 ||
May that auspicious Śivā ever proclaim my welfare— that very place where, by name, Ramā became known as "She Who Dwell in the Lotus Mansion" due to her eternal residence there.
Whose immeasurable majesty arises from the water of his feet.

May Lalitā Gaurī, the mistress of the palace of the Lord’s beautiful command, accept these compositions of the poet who serves her lotus feet, which extend from her hair down to her lotus feet. 10.25.
Description from the feet to the hair (in Āryā meter):
May the gentle smile of the Daughter of the Mountain, to which the Fish-bannered One directed a handful of enchanting powder upon Śiva, bring the world under our control. 11.1.
O Mother, when I strive to compare your limbs to the beautiful things in this world that subsist on but a mere fraction of your splendor, I am mostly overcome by shame.

I go for refuge to the left foot of the enemy of Kama’s consort, which bears upon the head of her whose brows are curved like Vedic scriptures the likeness of a fresh sprout worn as an ear-ornament. 11.3.
O wise one, your pair of shanks, which utterly intoxicates the eyes of Śiva and is exceedingly sweet, shines as the very treasure of the flower-arrowed god when described by the learned.
In each world, O Goddess, there is a pair that serves as the cause for mutual remembrance:
your broad thigh and the trunk of the elephant-faced Lord Bhava.
O Sovereign Lady, heaven clings to Your waist, the earth is the hip of the serpents, and the navel is the world;
indeed, the three worlds are not only within Your belly but also upon Your body. 11.6
O daughter of the Mountain, I consider your braid to be the great sword of Madana;
I suspect the line of hair on your body to be his razor-sharp-edged dagger.
Victorious is the pair of breasts of the Mother, from which the inexhaustible nectar of milk was drunk by the elephant-faced one, then by the six-faced one, and finally by the entire world.
O Mother of the World, your pair of arms, hanging down from your neck on both sides, shines like a beautiful garland of densely woven flowers.
The Asuras know your power; your friends know your exquisite beauty; the sages know your generosity;
and that God, the destroyer of the cities, O Mother, knows the softness of your hand.

O Mother, your throat— which resembles a conch shell, which is adorned with the ornaments of the world’s jewels and the garland of stars, and which possesses faultless sound— is a delight to the eyes and ears of Dhūrjaṭi’s arms.
O beloved of Hara, gazing again and again at your face, the moon that serves as your crest-ornament, though full, has become thin; it has likely withered away out of envy.
Let the entire class of faces of fickle-eyed women challenge the moon for battle;
yet, O beloved of Maheśa, your face alone has conquered it by its splendor.
O Goddess, your lotus-face, having surpassed the nectar-rayed moon that was proud of its victory over the lotus-born Brahmā,
has brought forth great and stainless fame for the entire lotus species.
Victorious is the charming lotus-face of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, which causes the world-bees to wander all around in the hope of its nectar of loveliness. 11.15.
O Bhavānī, your half-face, consisting of your forehead, was fashioned from the essence of the pure moon;
the other half was fashioned by the Creator from the essence of all that is beautiful.
O Daughter of the Mountain, your face has granted the path to its gateway to the moon, which has bowed down in defeat before it; here, your lower lip is the threshold for that gentle smile.
"Let those virtuous ones describe your eyes, your earrings, your necklace, and your crown;
we poets, O Goddess, describe your smile as the white-rayed moon. (11.18)
Who indeed is able to describe the splendor of the Mother’s bimba-fruit-like lips, which, having entered even within, spreads passion for the Lord of the Pramathas? 11.19
O Mother, you hold nectar for Gaṇapati in your two breasts, for the devotees of the seven worlds in your lotus feet, and for the conqueror of Tripura in the hollow of your lower lip. 11.20.
O Śivā, when the bridge of the nose has been constructed by the Creator over the river of the nectar of your gaze, the movement of your radiance in your face becomes free from all fear.

O Mother, may those two eyes of yours—your abode for the play of Lakṣmī and the home for the sport of compassion—be ever victorious, O beloved of Hari, who are so beautiful and devoted to the welfare of the humble. 11.22.

O Goddess, beloved of the lineage of the Moon-crested Lord, all your limbs are glorious; yet your two ears alone are the objects of praise for the multitude of poets, being as if they were the very embodiments of splendor.
O daughter, even your hair—crooked, soiled, and yet innocent—captivates the heart of the Lord of the World, the protector of the mountain (Indra), as it bears certain flowers. 11.24.
May these Āryā verses, which sing of the supreme beauty of Śambhu from his feet to the tips of his hair, be accepted by the lotus-eyed son of Atri. 11.25.
Description of the Erotic Sentiment (composed in the Rathoddhatā meter):

May the gentle smile of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains—the razor that shaves away the quality of Śiva’s fortitude, the banner-cloth for the victory over Śambara’s enemy, and the bud of intoxication—dispel my calamity. 12.1.

Once, O lady of lovely limbs, he whose crest is the young moon wandered over the grounds of the Silver Mountain, grasping your hand with his own, which was adorned with bracelets from which the jewels had been removed.
O Pārvatī, as he wandered all around there, a young bee—its luster resembling your own curls—was captivated by your beloved as she kissed a *vakula* flower; it stirred his heart.
Scratching his beloved, whose eyes were tremulous and beautiful, with the tip of his horn upon her body,
the deer delighted the mind of Dhūrjaṭi with glances that resembled yours.
The breezes, fragrant with the pollen of *mālatī* flowers from the groves of Mañjukuñja, and the tender, sweet warbling of young cuckoos, O Sovereign Lady, brought about the infatuation of Śiva.
O daughter of the mountain king, with creepers adorned with flowers before you and on both sides,
and with the sound of Cupid’s bowstring everywhere, how indeed can his composure endure?

O Mother, in the forest filled with the warbling of cuckoos, the fish-bannered god (Kāmadeva) struck Śambhu as he stood by your side with his arrows; for enemies indeed strike when the opportunity arises.
Struck by the god whose banner is the sea-monster, and resting his hand upon her shoulder,
Śaṅkara spoke thus to you, O lady with eyes like those of a yearling fawn.
Perched upon a young mango tree, this cuckoo utters a sweet, warbling cry;
O lotus-eyed one, let her release her lofty pride and pour forth her voice.
O slender one, the young breezes, carrying the nectar of full-blown kunda flowers and bearing the pollen of jasmine buds,
cause both the sprouts and my heart to tremble.

O beloved, I, a child, worship those limbs of yours—possessing a most serene and sweet form—which have stolen the eyes of Śrī with their description, or which are like the wind that removes drops of perspiration. 12.11.
O lady of faultless limbs, this peacock feather brings joy to my heart only so long as this loosened mass of your braided hair does not enter the path of my vision.

"O beloved, although this lower lip constantly stays near the stainless teeth, not even the slightest trace of its own quality has departed from it due to living together with them; for it remains full of passion."
O lady with beautiful teeth, your kinship is with the night-lilies at night and with the day-lotuses by day;
you are like a twice-born man of the earth who belongs to two lineages—the Kaśyapas and the Vasiṣṭhas.

With even a slight, yet exceedingly powerful, moonlight of a smile, his face— a lunar orb free from frost— dispels the darkness reaching to the heavens while scattering only the nectar of well-spoken words.

O lotus-faced one, your pair of breasts is like a pair of cakravāka birds on dry land, eternally free from the fear of night, closely joined to one another, and dwelling within the cottage of your firm garment.
O daughter of the mountain and Indra, does that pair of tender, sprout-like feet, which ought to be cherished by the crowns of the gods, not suffer from the harsh ground? (12.17)
While you, O daughter of the great mountain king, sat with your face sealed in silence as the Three-eyed Lord spoke these and other words, the god whose banner bears the water-bird performed a dance.
O Goddess, your hair is adorned with the garland of *pārijāta* flowers by the Conqueror of Cities;
yet it is remembered that his own mind was captivated by this very garland—where else has such a deed been performed by one of soiled soul?
If the heroine, steadfast due to her vow of celibacy,
is the crusher of the buffalo-demon, and the hero is the slayer of the flower-arrowed god, who could know the secret of our love?
Skilled in the rite that is a festival for the eyes, free from the defect of being veiled by clouds,
and possessing a beautiful form devoid of darkness, it dispels even the gloom situated in the sky.

O lady of auspicious limbs, what night was not a source of joy for you when the moon shone upon the slopes of the white mountain, which serves as a cottage for the matted locks of your life’s lord? 12.22.
May those various sports of Girijā and Giriśa, whose lovely faces mutually reveal their splendor through the rays of the moon that serves as their ornament, lead to the prosperity of the world.

O Mother, was there some playful sport on your part for the creation of one other than Modaka? O Sovereign Lady, was there some play for the birth of your jewel of a son, the wielder of power? (12.24)
May these Rathoddhatā verses of the learned Kavyakantha, overflowing with the essence of sweetness, bestow an indescribable and supreme joy upon the mind of the daughter of the Mountain Lord. 12.25.
May the wondrous smile of the Mother of the Elephant-Faced One ferry you across the ocean of existence; may her sidelong glance do the same. (In the Upajāti meter)
He who, even when transgressing against her bimba-red lips, clearly manifests his languid grace, dispels the darkness of the quarters.
Always attached to the collection of moonbeams,
bestowing compassion upon all beings—
he is either Gaurī’s sidelong glance, her lover, or a sage.
May he dispel my ignorance. || 13.2 ||
May the compassionate glance of the Daughter of the Mountain purify my inner self,
by which Śaṅkara is marked as the single reality.
He beheld the universe and proclaimed it to the world. || 13.3 ||
May Kālī’s sidelong glance bestow upon me words that liberate one from the intoxication of worldly existence— words by whose falling touch the author of the Raghuvaṃśa was purified.
They say that the woman is the human form of the Unborn.
May this deer-eyed consort of Giriśa extend her speech as the foremost among you;
for this manifold play of my words is the spreading power of her sidelong glance.
The flowing stream of the daughter of the mountain’s side-long glances, abounding in waves of compassion,
[cooled] those tormented by Bhīṣma, who bears the name of Bhava.
May summer make you cool. 13.6.
Just as Bhava’s head is perpetually moistened by the river Gaṅgā flowing through his inner being,
may Bhavasundarī bring peace from my burning anguish.
May he look upon me with a cool glance. || 13.7 ||
O Daughter of the Lord of the Kulācala mountains, even though she is always devoted solely to her husband, Puṇyā’s gaze is equal to yours, O Pativratā.
May he bring about the withdrawal of the spreading of calamities. || 13.8 ||
Deprived of restraint by Śarva,
your dark-eyed glance falls even upon a lowly mortal like a courtesan’s, though it is itself priceless.
He who possesses sixteen gold pieces.
O lotus-eyed daughter of the Earth,
this black serpent named "your sidelong glance" bites at the entire world.
And alas! Having forgotten, he does not maintain his composure through delusion. || 13.10 ||
O daughter of Mahendra, she who is like a mountain, forms a friendship with the wielder of the five arrows (Kāma) despite his being her enemy,
and she speaks in favor of sinners as well.
O Mother, why is your charming sidelong glance not directed toward me? 13.11
Endowed with compassion, moving near Karṇa, glorious, and always favorable toward the Puṇyajanas,
he possesses an equality with Śambhu, the lord of the Kurus.
Your sidelong glance favors one who is dearer to you than life itself. || 13.12 ||
Though standing at the very edge of his ear, the enemy of Dharma does not protect the clan of the Matsyas, even though he is Kṛṣṇa;
though cold, he kindles the fire of passion.
O daughter of the mountain, may your sidelong glance belong to Hara.
This side-glance of yours, a torrent of water expanding at the time of compassion,
leaves behind those dwelling happily in their homes.
O Mother of the Universe, you sprinkle those who are without support. || 13.14 ||
The commands of that person, equal to all others in speech, form, and power,
do not falter even at the shores of the ocean.
O beloved of Śambhu, this is the grace of your glance. || 13.15 ||
At their gates wander heroes;
within their palaces are young women with eyes like deer;
and in their assemblies are poets of bold speech.
All those upon whom your compassionate glance falls. || 13.16 ||
O Mother, wherever there is even a slight trace of one of Your sidelong glances, that hero becomes invincible on the field of battle;
first he fills heaven with his enemies, and thereafter he fills the earth with his moon-white fame.
He whom you do not behold, though he is as lovely as a cluster of stars, no one beholds;
yet even by him whom you behold, you are beheld.
The world attains abundant prosperity. || 13.18 ||
Mocking nectar, casting aside honey, and stealing away the fame of a woman’s lip,
this stream of his poetry adorns him.
O beloved of Hara, you look upon that face.
She who brings joy to all the senses, the pure woman, the faultless knowledge, and the vast fortune—
this Triple Gem belongs to that man.
O Durgā, we know that this has been seen by you.
O Daughter of the Mountain, you cast your glances in vain upon the trees of the Kailāsa forest;
were they to scatter [the flowers] from here, there would be no loss to you.
And all that he desires is accomplished for him. || 13.21 ||
O Kumārī, sovereign of the Snowy Mountain, you are cool in protecting those humans who have sought refuge in you,
yet fierce in the crushing of the irrepressible and wicked asuras.
And your glance is exceedingly hot.
Accompanied by anger, it brings about destruction;
accompanied by compassion, it provides nourishment and protection—
just like the glance of the physician Amba.
Through the differentiation of yoga, there is a differentiation of the qualities. || 13.23 ||

O beloved of Śiva, for the destruction of this disease of worldly existence—whose three humors of passion, greed, and anger are equally provoked—I would purchase your glance as a medicine; tell me, sir, for how much devotion shall I buy it? (13.24)

May the beautiful verses of the son of Mṛtyu, praised by throngs of Cāraṇas and Siddhas, and which purify those who bow down through the compassionate side-glances of the matted-haired Lord (Śiva), delight us even more than the various types of Triṣṭubh meters. 13.25.

May the gentle smile of the beautiful-eyed consort of Maheśvara—she who is Kālī, Gaurī, and Kuṇḍalinī; the cause of all supreme intellects and the dispeller of the darkness dwelling within—be for my well-being. (In the Upagīti meter) 14.1.

Victorious is Kālī, Gaurī, Ambikā—the one whose body is the universe yet whose limbs are slender, who is composed of thunderbolts yet delicate as a flower, the power of all, appearing as a woman. 14.2.
Some call her Gaurī, the Mother of the World; others, Kālī.
That Gaurī has the body of a woman, while Kālī is said to have the body of the sky.
Time is distinguished from the power of cooking (the goddess Kālī) solely by its mark; for it is through time’s ripening that all transformations occur in the world. 14.4

Because she is the support of all worlds, she is named Kālī by another [name]; however, the worldly usage of the terms "direction" and "time" among the learned is merely figurative with respect to direction and time.

Kālī is remembered as the undivided source of the quarters, the transformer of all; she is the one daughter of Dakṣa, appearing as two to those whose vision is deluded by the distinctions of the *guṇas*.
In every body, she is this one known as Kuṇḍalinī, the Mother of the World;
she sleeps for those caught in the cycle of worldly existence, but she becomes awakened for those who practice yoga.
Fire blazes from the *mūlādhāra* and the moon melts from the head;
O Mother Kuṇḍalinī, I believe she has awakened from her bed of the lute. 14.8.
What is it that flows there? What is it that you are there where it burns?
O Maheśvarī, what indeed are you there where both of these are known?
May these two, Agni and Soma, envelop my body with their flames and their moonlight; may I become the manifestation of these two. 14.10.
You are Agni, you are Soma; you blaze below and you flow above.
You are the nectar that is the fruit of these two, and you, O Mother Consciousness, are its enjoyer. 14.11
O Sovereign of all, what good deed have I performed, or what austerity have I practiced, that You play with me at every moment within this ocean of the nectar of bliss? (14.12)
"Have you forgiven my transgression? Is your heart at peace, O Queen?
You show me such varied favor, even though I am the foremost among offenders. (14.13)
At the proper times, the twilight devotions were not performed;
how then could the Smārta fire of the threefold sacrificial fires remain unextinguished?
I have not earned enough food to give to the gods and the spirits;
whatever little I have earned, I eat together with my wife and sons. (14.15)
O Mother of the World, you have not removed any of my sins, nor have you performed the preliminary rites for your mantra; with what quality in view do you awaken within me? 14.16
If this partiality toward me is due to your love for your own son,
then O Mother, this must be considered as the natural disposition of the virtuous toward you.
Without an object, can a mantra achieve success even if recited ten million times?
If we blow [the conch] toward that object—your form—alas, the mantra dissolves! 14.18
That which is the root of volitions, words, and experiences;
that wherein the vital breath is bound—that, O Goddess, is your form as the object of focus.
Having sought the root of the ego, which is the natural function of one's own being, [one finds it there].
Indeed, this vision of the great seer Raṇamaṇa beholds you directly.
"O Daughter of the Mountain, I believe this great sense of self-importance of mine has its root in that [attainment]; alas, even after descending for many years, it has not been found. (14.21)
O Blessed One, this mature egoism roars loudly;
and at this very time, you have awakened as Kuṇḍalinī.
Even now he does not know that his own birth shall follow after yours;
yet, as before, he roars with confidence, fearing not death even when it is closest at hand.
O Mistress of the life-force of the Lord of the Pramathas, this Gaṇapati, your exclusive devotee, offers to you this animal whose ego is exceedingly nourished. 14.24.

May these Upagītis, out of affection, attend upon the Mistress of the House of Him who is called by the sound "U," and who is eager for thousands of festivals, as they do for the Lord of the Gaṇas. 14.25.
Welcome to Śakti!
May she remove our multitude of calamities and grant us the abundance of prosperity.
The smiles of the fair-eyed consort of Śiva bestow strength through the luster of her pearl-like teeth.
Though slight, it was enriched with extraordinary power; though gentle, it spread with exceptional subtlety—
the beautiful smile of the woman who is the enemy of the God of Love.
May it be conducive to the welfare of my family. || 15.2 ||
Moving from Puṣkara to the Sun, and from the Earth to the Moon,
alas, she does not let go of her previous step.
She does not go to the next world, nor is she the mistress of her own house. || 15.3 ||
O Mother, like gold in ornaments,
or like clay in all jars,
you are that which is devoid of distinctions within all things in the universe.
O Goddess, the wise one beholds you as the virtuous Satī.

When the entire collection of the vital breath, intellect, and mind has reached its final digestion within her own digestive fire, the whole world of the visible becomes mere waste for the consort of the Lord of All.
"He is the very essence"—thus is the saying of the wise. 15.5.
O Sovereign, those who, through the churning of their intellect, perceive You as the one essence hidden within all bodies, just as oil is hidden within sesame seeds;
They become the enlightened ones, merged within you. || 15.6 ||
O Mistress of the Three Worlds, the physical body of that person whose subtle body consists of the blazing net of consciousness becomes like iron through the heat of his asceticism, as if by fire.
O Mother, that [world] which was once your abode has become scorched.
He who, free from blemish, kindles the vital breath from his own body— just as one without stain produces the most pure fire by the friction of fire-sticks.
O Giver of Fearlessness, this person deserves to sacrifice to you.
By one who breathes, only the breathing itself should be investigated;
by one who acts, only the act itself should be observed; by one who goes, only the going itself should be purified.
The churning within one's own body is to be understood through the scriptures.
O Sovereign of All, he who drinks the nectar from the lotus of his crown, being self-restrained and sinless, is a drinker of Soma;
this is his constant fire-sacrifice.
Its state is that of burning the root-pit. || 15.10 ||
Consisting of consciousness, you drink this Soma; are you the Soma itself, or are you its Mother? You alone are both that which is drunk and that which drinks.
Having become what, indeed, is this pair of vessels for drinking? || 15.11 ||
Just as gold of a fiery nature, when heated by fire, becomes nothing but light, O lady with limbs of golden hue,
so too has [this world] been heated by the digit of your form of bliss.
That mass of joy becomes identical with it. || 15.12 ||
O Mother, some wave of Your essence has emerged from the ocean of the nectar of the thousand-spoked wheel;
it fills my entire body, yet I do not perceive any part here that remains insentient. 15.13
O Queen of all, this most excellent [light], falling from the cool cloud of the thousand-rayed moon,
has been sent forth by you.
The rain of aesthetic flavor descends upon the crop of the intellect.

Just as nectar is obtained from the churning of the ocean of milk, or the *praṇava* from the churning of the ocean of sound, so too is this essence— the wave of Your speech— attained by the virtuous through the churning of the lotus of their heads.
Flowing with great force through the bones,
bestowing the nectar-essence of marrow,
she carries a joy that is neither hot nor free from defect.
Your stream [is] in the abode of the lotus upon the crown [of my head]. || 15.16 ||
This very attainment of the essence described in the Taittirīya is that which is praised in all the Āgamas;
this alone [is found] when the Moon is the lord of the lunar disc.
The drinking of the supreme nectar spoken of in the Tantras. || 15.17 ||
O beautiful consort of Śambhu, having pressed the moon upon my head with hands joined in the gaze of the ageless and immortal form, I offer libations and I satisfy [thee].
You, who have entered the dwelling of the blazing sacrificial fire-pit of the family.
The fierce rays of the sun, her very gaze,
entering the moon of her lotus-head,
indeed become composed of cool nectar.
O Yoginī, your digit of delight flows forth.
O Consort of Śaṅkara, you flow upon the heads of those joined in yoga, you blaze in their eyes,
and you abide with firm footing in the kula-kuṇḍa.
You never stumble at all on the outside. || 15.20||
If she flows, she would be the essence of joy; if she blazes, she would be the spark of consciousness.
If she remains as the supreme, firm state, she becomes some kind of imperishable existence.
O daughter of the mountain king, you are perceived by me as I observe the movement of the circle of my eyes,
knowing the play of the thousand petals of the lotus.
O Mother, you have touched upon that which is known as a secret.
Shining with the vital strength of pervasive power,
scorching with eyes like the orb of the sun,
and sporting with a mind fixed on the orb of the moon.
She, moreover, triumphs while dwelling upon the crown of the head. || 15.23 ||
Welcome to you, who are honored by all the worlds; welcome to you, the queen of the king of the universe;
welcome to you, who are exceedingly compassionate toward me.
Welcome to the Perfection of Wisdom in Ten Thousand Lines!
O King, may this welcome from me— composed in these charming, faultless verses by a true poet—
be spoken as a greeting to you.
This head is for play, for the sake of going to the beyond. || 15.25 ||

May the smile of the Great Lord’s consort, which dispels the great delusion within and possesses the majesty of inner power— may it spread the foremost festival within my home. 16.1 (In the Kumāralalitā meter)
Bearing this world, so vast in its multitude of spheres yet so light,
she whose ordinances remain unbroken even by the faces of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Bestowing auspicious things upon those of unblemished conduct, she brings ruin to the families of the corrupt. (16.3)
Wearing a silk garment with the luster of crimson rays,
she is dependent upon Hara, the sovereign of the Silver Mountain.
May Umā, who has bestowed many gifts renowned in the tantras composed by the Lord of Munis, and whose majesty is incomparable, grant us sufficient strength. 16.5.
That you maintain this pillar of thought fixed upon the Lord of the entire world, having cast aside all other objects—this is your steadfastness. 16.6
When heard, you incline the mind; when remembered, you make a man sinless;
when held in the heart, you bestow upon one who has transcended the distinction between self and other.
"To the virtuous, you alone are indeed the very root of the earth for the river of the ego-sense"— such is the speech of the beloved of the great sage.
O Mother, O Consort of the Lord, when the creeper of the ego-sense is rooted in You,
who are the bulbous root of the world, one attains the secret of the universe.
O Mother of all, this entire world which appears as if it were real is indeed Your own net; one who has entered it speaks of You as its very root.
You perceive the world with its manifold divisions as something external;
yet, in the inward Self, there is nothing other than that which is before you.
You are praised eternally and remembered in worship;
you are sustained in yoga and expanded in awakening.
When praised, you grant one’s desires; when remembered, you take away sin; when held in the heart, you provide supreme power; and when expanded [through meditation], you become liberation itself.
One who is restrained in their conduct is purified; one who is pure does not fall into negligence.
For one free from negligence, you shine forth clearly in the blossomed lotus.
O Mother of the World, if you clearly perform a skillful dance like an actress upon the head of one whose intellect is disciplined, it is as if a lotus has blossomed. 16.15
O Mother, this lotus upon our heads is in full bloom;
it possesses abundant nectar—be you the female bee.
O Mother, drink the nectar while nibbling at the lotus;
O great honeybee, you shall experience intense intoxication.
"O Consort of the Lord, until now I have experienced only inauspiciousness;
from this point forward, may you experience supreme joys."
O Sovereign Consciousness, by the power of egoism, I was once [separate] from you;
now, however, I possess no independent sovereignty.
When she was mine, she experienced distress;
O Goddess, may she now experience joy while being yours. 16.20.
Let this "I-ness" continue its dispute even now;
