nevertheless, O Maheśvarī, it remains utterly powerless in Your presence.
And since this activity of your intellect arises from this [anger],
O patient one, free yourself from resentment and perform even this [act of forgiveness] toward yourself.
O Mother, here is an ocean of nectar garlanded with hundreds of waves;
here is a city of the clouds of consciousness, a boundless abode of splendor.
O Sāvitrī, perform this one task among your hundreds of dwellings:
sport as you please within this body.
May this work of Gaṇapati, composed in the Kumāralalitā meter, bring joy to the beloved of Kapardin. 16.25.

May that indescribable power of intoxication— the stainless Gaṅgā for the washing away of sins, the moonbeam for the dispelling of heat, and the art of laughter of Bharga’s consort— grant me unmixed auspiciousness. (In the Campakamālā meter) 17.1.
May she, the Queen of the Universe, who brings joy to the families of the virtuous and quiets the wicked, dispel the boundless suffering of me, her devotee. 17.2.

I praise that woman of pure conduct, whose feet resemble the orb of the newly risen sun, whose lotus-face rivals the cool-rayed moon, who possesses renowned majesty, and who is the enemy of the flower-arrowed god of love. 17.3.
Shining in the sky of radiant stars, gleaming like the moon, and burning with heat, may she who creates contemplation through her cool rays and who sustains the world protect my lineage. 17.4

May that certain manifestation of the Creator of the world—a manifestation consisting of the separated powers of breath, mind, and speech, and taking the form of the lotus, the earth, and fire—render our sins utterly dry. (17.5)
O Mother, for the fulfillment of desired fruits and for the instantaneous destruction of those with bitter results,
I praise you, O Sovereign of the World, whose power is kindled by even the slightest movement.

O Mother, it is said that you bestow your abode upon him who, having placed his vessel upon the tip of a tree and drinking honey again and again incessantly, rejoices while forgetting the entire world.
"O Goddess, this one who vomits forth from his thousands of mouths that which you protect within my body is the praiseworthy Śeṣa, the king of serpents. (17.8)
O immeasurable Goddess, as long as my ego remains uncast aside by you,
so long will this stream from the belching of the king of serpents continue to stupefy it, O Sovereign.
Thought ceases, life in this [body] comes to an end, and even the existence of the senses sets;
alas, O Mother, this slayer of mine has reached the throat and is on the verge of death.
O Gaurī, friend of the life-breath of Maheśa, protect me, your fallen mother;
O Īśvarī, if she should live, this servant of yours shall offer her back to you.

O Mother, what hesitation can there be for you, whose mind is at peace, now to make me—through the power of remembering you—a servant of your own self, endowed with tranquility and supremely pure? 17.12.
The Mandara mountain is not the cause of the nectar, nor is Vāsuki the rope the cause of the nectar;
rather, it is the act of churning that is the cause of the nectar—she who is the soul of all power, the consort of Śarva.
The body of a living being is Mount Mandara; the root-lotus is the king of tortoises;
the full and infinite milk-ocean is the back; and the bowstring is the serpent Vāsuki. || 17.14 ||
The right channel is the army of the gods, and the leftward channel is the army of the demons;
the play of Śakti is the act of churning, and the stream from the head is called some kind of nectar.
O Goddess, when the poison and fire have greatly obstructed the throat, who here could remain a ghost after drinking the sweet nectar born of your power, which dwells within the fiery liṅga of Hara?

O Primordial One, increase that intoxication which causes Śarva to rejoice in his splendor and in which you, O Śivā, sport joyfully; for that intoxication is the root of rapture, and it should be fostered in your son, who is a worthy recipient of your grace.

He who, having disregarded such a path as this, is filled with pride toward those honored by the lords of heaven, and seeks to acquire wealth through external riches or liquor—he is called an *asura*. (17.18)
He who indulges in intense froth faints; he who indulges in the leaf of consciousness grows weary;
he who indulges in vessels of liquor wanders astray; he who indulges in head-liquefiers finds peace.
May it be wholesome for purgation; may its leaf be used when there is indigestion;
may that wine be beneficial in cases of consumption—O Goddess, your nectar brings an end to the cycle of rebirth.
O Mother, let even those great beings who are abundant in spiritual power waver in all intoxicants;
for the consumption of intoxicating substances by the small-minded is said to be their destruction.
O Mistress of the Life of the Enemy of Tripura, some worship you with honey and meat;
yet in this case, the sacrifice is not subject to reproach, for it is the sacrificer who is defiled by attachment to material substances.
On the southern path the devotee attains success; on the leftward path the hero attains success.
O Goddess, neither on the left nor on the right is success attained; rather, the silent sage attains success on the divine path.
In this most auspicious divine path, there is no burden of ritual worship nor the need for recitation;
one must simply seek the lotus feet of the Mother incessantly with an unwavering mind.
May this priceless Campaka garland, a beautiful wreath composed in verse, become a Campaka garland dangling upon the neck of Gaṇeśa, the beloved of the Lord. 17.25.

The particular forms and the radiant manifestation of Kuṇḍalinī— (in the Prahārṣiṇī meter)— shaking off the mass of darkness from the slopes of the directions and delighting the eyes of the Destroyer of Cities;
May the smiles of Skanda’s mother, radiant with white light, forcibly and instantly remove the dense delusion residing within my heart. 18.1.
Spreading what is beneficial for the humble, shaking the ranks of adversaries, and bestowing joy upon wise men—
may she be the sovereign queen of the heavens, the earth, and the netherworld.
May Rudrāṇī, the auspicious one, speak for my lineage. || 18.2 ||
O Mother, he who places you— who shine like lightning, possess the luster of nectar, and have a face-lotus that steals away pride— in his heart,
shakes off everything else from the path of his memory.
O fair-toothed one, for the enemy of Kama who bows upon the earth, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. || 18.3 ||

O Consort of Bharga, that steadfast one who holds in his mind [the Goddess] whose essence and power are unequaled to the luster of a dark cloud, and whose fierce white fangs cause the waves of the Śakti to whirl; [he shall attain liberation].
In battles, his weapon is subject to you alone. 18.4.

O slender-limbed one, those wise men who meditate upon you, whose body is radiant as the rising sun, bear the command of the Conqueror of Tripura upon their heads— just as those dwelling on earth remain subject to one who wears a garland of full-blown jasmine.
I bow to you, who, with the lotus of your hand, hold a book as white as the essence of the moon’s luster,
and who constantly awaken the Lord Bhūteśa.
Or, by meditating [on her], Vāgadūtī becomes subject to his control. 18.6.
O Blessed One, we know that you instantly assume a supreme form equal to the mental disposition of your devotee.
O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, this question arises: what kind of form of yours intoxicates even the enemy of Smara? (18.7)
O Mother, it is impossible for anyone to say whether your form is "beautiful" or "sufficient," nor can they describe what kind it is; rather,
people fall into a state of supreme bewilderment before that vessel of splendor.
Wherein even the eyes of the Enemy of Kāma are fixed upon that which is seen.
Did my mental constructs become your ornaments, or did the lords of craftsmen fashion them here in this world?
O Blessed One, what kind of gold is that, and what is the nature of the jewels set therein? (18.9)

O Umā, what need have these limbs—which are themselves the essence of all that is beautiful—of ornaments? Or rather, do they not shine even more exquisitely when adorned with the most elaborate decorations? (18.10)
O Mother, is your necklace made of pearls as pure as the essence of the moon’s rays,
or rather of skulls that produce a "ghala-ghala" sound?
From the rivalry [of those two], O consort of the sovereign of the three worlds! || 18.11 ||
If your garment, which is known through all the scriptures, were made of cotton, then its origin would have to be inferred as being in heaven;
if it were made of linen, O Blessed One, then its causal source [would likewise be sought there].
It must be stated that there could even be insects in the expanse of the sky.

Or rather, O beloved wife of Rudra, he is capable and able to provide you with celestial trees fashioned from gems and gold, as well as garments most pleasing to the mind, according to your desire. (18.13)
O Blessed One, is this tree named Kalpa, with its sturdy trunk, many branches, beautiful with tender shoots, and filling the quarters with the fragrance of its fully blossomed flowers?
O Goddess, has some resolve of yours come true? 18.14
Neither the wish-fulfilling tree nor the celestial cow can produce these two things merely by thought; rather, it is she who,
through her exalted vital power, brings them both forth.
And by your compassion on this earth, he shall possess the fortune of heaven.
The thousand-petaled lotus becomes full;
its calf is the fire of the Kundalini at the root, most skillful;
the milker is the Self seated upon the small lotus of the heart.
There would be silence regarding the bodies of the gods and cows, and there would be milking [of the former]. || 18.16 ||
O Blessed One,
my soul, drinking the sweet nectar-like milk obtained by your milking of that cow whose first drink was the fire of the calf, is satisfied.
He is never satisfied; his belly is difficult to fill. || 18.17 ||
O Mother, the calf-like fire drinks with firm feet; thereafter, the inner self drinks incessantly while milking from the front.
And as each act of milking proceeds, the fluid increases; thus, O Kuṇḍalinī, your flow here is boundless.
Some call this liquid the essence of Soma; others say it is the nectar from the ocean of milk;
some, however, declare it to be the vapor from the Kaula-kunda.
Others say that the flow from the udder of a cow is "pīnodhas. || 18.19 ||
At the root, you are of the nature of the radiance of blazing petals;
in the lute, you are of the nature of the intense heat of great passion;
in the lotus of the head, you are of the nature of the nectar constantly flowing.
In the middle of the eyebrows, you abide as the nature of shimmering lightning.
If you descend here into the lotus of the heart,
you will perceive everything like a shadow;
O Daughter of the Mountain, you have ascended the thousand-petaled lotus.
If you were to call this world an ocean of nectar, [it would be so]. || 18.21 ||
With eyes as broad as lotus petals and a face radiant with a pure smile,
that woman stands before my mind as if visibly present.
The fortune of our lot has been won by the enemy of Kāma. || 18.22 ||
He is the very fruition of merits for the sustainer of beings, a certain secret treasury of power for the perfected ones,
and the most steadfast support for devotees in the ocean of sorrow.
My mother, the daughter of the mountain, is among the most exalted.
To lift up those who are bowed down from the pit of despair,
to refine those joined in yoga for the welfare of the world,
and to destroy the host of the wicked who are arrogant with pride—
The beloved young wife of Bharga is ever intent on constant contemplation.
Surpassing the grape in sweetness, nectar in its greatness, and the celestial river in its profundity, this poem,
devoted to the life of Śarvāṇī, is composed in the Prahārṣiṇī meter.
May this guild, established by Gaṇeśvara, be victorious!

May the smile of the beautiful consort of Maheśa—the form of Lalitā who is the object of meditation—dispel your great affliction; it steals away the splendor of the blossoming flowers of the wish-fulfilling tree. (In the Pramāṇikā meter) 19.1.
It is the awakening of Dhanañjaya, the foremost among the sages,
and the breaking of the bolt on the door-panel of the casket of the heart of the Lord of Ascetics.
May the smile of my Mother, which purifies the minds of others through the performance of rites according to the prescribed rules, become the obstruction to the power of my sins.
She was like a moving golden statue, surpassing all in beauty;
endowed with extreme softness, she was like a newly blossomed creeper.
Her golden sandals shone with the luster of the jewels in the crowns of the gods;
her excellent jeweled anklets were as if addressed by the female swans.
The rows of her toenails captivated by the excellence of the radiance of white moonbeams;
she whose exquisite feet were to be measured only by the pure minds of the lords of sages. 19.6
Her calves were like a continuous stream of condensed lightning radiance;
she was graced with beautiful thighs resembling the trunk of a lordly elephant.
Her lower garment was skilled in proclaiming the arrival of the flower-arrowed god [Kāma],
and her broad hips shone as they were kissed by her flowing hair.
Her belly was filled with the mass of unborn eggs,
and her navel-pool was a reservoir for the waters of boundless divine splendor.
Her line of body hair was like a garland of *bisaka* flowers serving as arrows;
her breasts, bearing milk, were the source of sustenance for the virtuous who dwell within the three worlds.
Her beautiful vine-like arms are praised for binding the neck of Maheśa,
and her lotus-like hands bestow fearlessness upon all the worlds.
Her smile harmonized with the clusters of pearls from her swaying necklace;
she illuminated the sky with the radiance of her pure and beautiful smile.
The invincible Asuras were terrified by the trembling of her very delicate lips;
her row of teeth shone with the brilliance of well-formed jasmine buds.
Her face surpassed the splendor of the autumnal orb of the moon,
and her lower lip was like a hibiscus flower dripping with nectar.
Her nose shone, mocking the beauty of a sesame flower;
from her fresh and radiant nose hung a divine pearl.
Her jeweled earrings reflected the form of her pure cheeks;
her eyes were magnificent, their radiance rippling with great splendor.
The ground was illuminated by the luster of the moon situated between the petals,
and she shone with hair that surpassed the beauty of a peacock’s plumage.
Resplendent with ten million suns, cool as a hundred thousand moons,
radiant with a thousand lightnings, and crowned by the moon without its spot.
Moving through the midst of the sky, performing many wondrous deeds,
she rests within the sacrificial fire-pit of the Kula and ordains the narrative of the universe.
In the vault of heaven she is Baleśvarī; on the surface of the earth she is Kriyeśvarī;
in the sun she is Vibheśvarī; and in the moon she is Raseśvarī.
She is the lamp illuminating the abode of Maheśa, the authority for the three worlds, the ruler of all heads, and the dweller within the hearts of all. || 19.21 ||
In every praise of her virtues, she bestows an excellence of qualities;
in every reflection upon her, she imparts a distinguished power.
Agitated by delusion, it is difficult to cross; for one weary of existence, it is hard to traverse; without counsel, it is difficult to sustain; and for the three worlds, it is invincible.
Clad in golden garments, the maker of all joy, playful and free from ailment—let her be meditated upon by you with your mind. 19.24.
May this *Pramāṇikāvalī*, composed by the poet who worships the lotus feet [of Śiva], become a source of great fortune in the home of the sovereign lady of Maheśa’s mind. 19.25.

Composed entirely of the essence of all things (in the maṇibandha meter), may the wondrous smile of the Creator of the Universe— which expands with joy and increases greatly even at the slightest sign of anger— protect the virtuous and slay the wicked. 20.1.

May she who brings joy to the hearts of the virtuous, who removes the multitude of sins of those who take refuge in her, who is the mother of the world, who dwells in heaven, and who bestows constant welfare—may she grant me prosperity again and again. 20.2.

At the time of worship, she resides in form; at the time of praise, she resides in sound; at the time of meditation, she resides in the vital breath; and during the investigation of reality, she is omnipresent. 20.3
In her radiant form she is the dancer; in her lusterless form she is the sleep-inducer.
In her concealed form she is the bestower of perfection; in her perceptible form she is the binder.
In Ambaradeśa she possesses sound; in Pāvakatāta she possesses touch;
in Kāñcanavīrya she possesses form; and in Sāgarakāñcī she possesses fragrance.
In the pure waters she is of clear flavor; in the radiance of the moon, her flavor is hidden.
In the enjoyment of worldly existence she possesses all flavors; in perfect meditative absorption, she is of a single flavor.
Vision in the eye is most clear; vision in the mind is most variegated.
Vision in the self is most pure; vision in Brahman is most complete.
The digit of the Moon is in the lotus of the head; the digit of Indra (the lightning) is in the lotus of the forehead;
the digit of the Sun is in the lotus of the heart; and the digit of Fire is in the root-lotus. 20.8.
In the gross body she is Kāntimatī; in the vital body, Śaktimatī; in the mental body, Bhogavatī; and in the intellectual body, Yogavatī. || 20.9 ||
The radiant luster of the friend of the cranes, the beautiful light of the friend of the night-lotuses,
the wondrous glow of the lightning-fire, and the illuminating brilliance of the earthly fire.
The splendor of weapons for the best of warriors, the splendor of eyes for the best of sages,
the splendor of thrones for kings, and the splendor of faces for those full of love.
The wielders of weapons possess ferocity; the wielders of scriptures possess the power of awakening.
The wielders of machines possess the power of movement; the wielders of mantras possess the power of accomplishment. 20.12
Those skilled in song possess the power to delight; those skilled in meditation possess the power to measure.
Those skilled in policy possess the power to divide; those skilled in asceticism possess the power to cast away.
A stream of rays for those who perceive, a stream of life for those who sustain it, a stream of knowledge for those who reflect, and a stream of intoxication for those who dissolve [in bliss]. 20.14.
For those devoted to mantras, there is the power of speech; for those devoted to yoga, the power of breath;
for those devoted to the self, the power of peace; and for those devoted to dharma, the power of renunciation.
The strength of the best of poets lies in their power of debate; the strength of the best of heroes lies in their arms;
the strength of lords of men lies in their armies; and the strength of passionate women lies in their laughter. 20.16.
In the Vedic mantra she is Bhāvavatī; in the Tantric mantra, Nādavatī;
in the Śabara mantra, Kalpavatī; and in the Santata mantra, Sāravatī. (20.17)
In the lotus-face of Brahmā she is Vāgvanitā; on the chest of Viṣṇu she is the graceful Śrī;
she has entered as a portion into the body of Śambhu; and she is spread throughout the sky, which is the body of the universe.
With the spheres of the earth and the planets as her ball, she is playful with the foundation of the world;
she possesses infinite majesty and abounds within all living beings.
In the egg-born from the lotus, she is Maṇḍalinī; in the bodies of living beings, she is Kuṇḍalinī;
in the state of the vulgar, she is Sallalanā; and in the state of the wise, she is Modaghanā.
A woman, though possessing roots through her man, is slender yet pervasive by virtue of her power;
being pervasive, she is hidden, a certain virtuous woman wondrously manifold.
She is the form of the *Dīdhiti* (the Light), consisting of consciousness, having the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as her body, yet non-dual;
she is the body of Brahman, the splendor of Brahman, the manifestation of Brahman, and the supreme Brahman.
The mother of the world, possessed of great compassion; the queen of the world, possessed of great power;
the embodiment of the world, praised by the disciplined; she who dwells beyond the world, measured by the perfected ones.
May Śivā protect our family of merit, which cuts down the root of the wicked, destroys the suffering of the distressed, and increases the wealth of wisdom and strength. 20.24.

May these verses of the Lord of Sages—which are pleasing to the ear and bound with excellent jewels—delight the hearts of those with lotus-eyes crowned by the moon, hearts already enriched with peace. 20.25.

Ardhanārīśvara (in the Anuṣṭubh meter): Having drunk from one breast here, while Skanda extends his hand toward the other, the smile arising from Śiva and Pārvatī, who share a single body, is victorious. 21.1.
On one side, white-winged birds were summoned by the tinkling of jeweled anklets; on the other, they were struck with fear by the hissing of the lord of serpents in his nūpura ornaments.
On one side, he fondled the child who was the protector of the host of gods;
on the other, he bore upon his lap the infant sovereign of the Gaṇas.
On one side, his chest bore the likeness of a single breast of a *koka* bird imitating a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), while on the other side it possessed the appearance of half a door-panel.
On one side was a fierce elephant, its milk tasted by the commander, yet not hissing; on the other side was another fierce elephant, wide awake and noisy with its trumpet-call.
On one side he bore a creeper-like arm that mocked the beauty of a lotus stalk,
and on the other, a fierce, staff-like arm resembling the trunk of a rutting elephant.
Even when there was no one worthy of worship present at any time,
they would join their palms in reverence out of a desire for the touch of each other's hands.
Because both parts possess a color like that of Indra’s sapphire, the region of the throat is known by its joint, which depends upon the upper and lower portions of the body. (21.8)
On one side, his eye was awakening the sleep of the rows of night-lotuses;
on the other, his gaze was bestowing a momentary dwelling upon the day-lotuses.
On one side was the beauty of her eye with its lovely pupil, possessing a studied grace;
on the other, a young fawn was playing with her lotus-like hand.
On one side, her forehead-slate was distinguished by saffron;
on the other, by a half-glance that destroys the playful movements of Rati’s eyebrows.
On one side was a cool light, bringing auspiciousness to virtuous people; on the other, a blazing glare, striking fear into the company of the wicked.
On one side, his cheek was washed by the luster of a jeweled earring;
on the other, it was encircled by a coiled earring.
On one side he bore locks of hair with a luster like sapphire,
and on the other, matted locks with clusters of rays as pale-red as the flames of a fire.
On one side, it was radiant with a mass of hair scattered across his chest; on the other, it stole the splendor of a serpent by means of its hanging folds.
On one side, he was adorned with a garland of unfading *pārijāta* flowers;
on the other, by the celestial river, whose waves were pure and surging.
May that reality, which has taken the form of women and men and whose abode is made of silver mountains, enter my heart when attained with a disciplined mind.
O Mother, upon your body which is half-formed with your beloved, your matted locks and half-bound hair possess the splendor of dark clouds joined with the dense clouds of twilight.
O Daughter of the Mountain, this is the loss for you two, a young couple: that the Lord has no left side for you to occupy, nor does he have his right hand to give to you. (21.19)
In this world, a woman nourishes either one son with her pair of breasts, or perhaps none at all;
yet you, O Śarvāṇī, nourish the three worlds with but a single breast.
Women grow weary carrying a single child in their womb;
yet you, O Mother, effortlessly hold the three worlds within half of your womb. 21.21.
You are a worthy match for Śiva, and Śiva is a worthy match for you;
the spotless young moon is a fitting ornament for the left side.
You alone are a portion of your own body; you belong to Hara, as he belongs to Hara.
O Sustainer of the worlds, you are the life-breath of Hara, and Hara is yours.
O Bhavānī, your own self is undivided from that of Bhava;
may your compassionate mind once and for all intend auspiciousness for us both.
Having relinquished her share of existence, Bhavānī shall enjoy her own share among these *anuṣṭubh* verses created by Nārasiṃha.

The gentle smile of her whose eyes are like the lotus of Śiva—she who is the cause of blossoming for all, and our protector among those afflicted by adversity and the wise—may she especially bestow auspiciousness upon us. 22.1. (In the Viyoginī meter) Harakuṭumbakam.
When the entire host of gods had turned dark-complexioned before Acyuta,
he who was compassionate toward the world swallowed the Hālāhala poison in a single mouthful and dispelled their fear.
He who, with the Vedas as his horses, the earth as his chariot, and the Creator as his charioteer,
shattered the three cities with the golden mountain as his bow and the lotus-eyed Lord as his arrow.

And he who, by the force of the stream from his lotus-weaponed foot, swiftly brought about the slaughter of Jalandhara, against whom the gods, led by the Lord of Kamalā and overcome by intense envy, were powerless.
Alas, even though they strive as the swan and the boar incarnations, the lotus-seated Brahmā and the dark-eyed Viṣṇu are not able to behold the head and feet of this deceptive form.
He, who— having slightly opened his eye situated between his brows while possessed by a touch of wrath—
consumed Madana, who was arrogant from his conquest of the three worlds and deeply intoxicated.
In its entirety white, yet in some parts as beautiful as a sapphire,
he bestows upon those who behold him a supreme joy to the eyes, like the moon.
The expanse of the quarters, rendered exceedingly pure by both the splendor of the moon serving as his crest-ornament and the abundance of his fame, shines forth most brilliantly.
Alas, this great world is pervaded on all sides by his eight forms: ether, fire, water, air, earth, moon, sun, and the sacrificer.

Together with that husband, O upholder of the earth, there shines a certain woman who is resplendent, who destroys the suffering of her lord, and who eats only what is offered by the servants at his feet. 22.10.
The ancient couple, the divine husband and wife in the stainless sky, are the lords of the three worlds; here on the Silver Mountain, they are the perfected husband and wife.
Wearing an elephant hide and holding a skull-cup, the Lord of the House (Śiva) and his consort Kālikā—garlanded with blood-stained heads—are indeed declared by the wise to be Śiva and Śivā. 22.12.
Is he the one who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, or is he adorned with the skull of a corpse?
Are you the bearer of skulls, or are you resplendent with a garland of jewels? (22.13)
O Mother, you sport sometimes with the Lord who wears a garland of skulls, and sometimes with him who wears a necklace of incomparable radiance and a most excellent garland of jewels.
O Mother, your sons born of you, the Maruts, are powerful and shakers of the world;
their purifying fame, which captivates even the rays of the moon, is sung in the Veda.

O Goddess Śivā, they declare your supreme Guru to be one of the Maruts, the sons of your body, the leader of those who move through the clouds and the peerless presiding deity over the treasure of the Vedas.
In his face, they saw an elephant in great rut, its white tusks washing the horizons with their luster;
elsewhere, from his mouth, they perceived a human form—a wondrous transformation of Vidura himself.
The powerful Dānava Tāraka, who had been exalted by his victory over all the immortals,
was instantly stripped of his pride in his prowess by the splendor of the weapon Śakti wielded by him.

He of boundless majesty reveals the further shore of darkness to that man whose heart is pure, whose cravings have been cleansed, whose knots of ignorance are loosened, and whose intellect is fully ripened. (22.19)

Having attained childhood among the Dravidas, he composed a hymn of praise that took on the luster of the Vedas, which was filled with specific verses to Giriśa and captured the essence of the flow of nectar.

On earth, having come into existence under the name Bhaṭṭakumārilā, he indeed established— through many logical arguments— the intended meaning of the teachings spoken by the venerable Jaimini, for the sake of protecting the sacrificial rites.
Now he who, wearing the guise of the great sage named Ramaṇa and dwelling in the beautiful caves of the Śoṇācala mountain, dispels the darkness that obstructs the path perceived by the wise. (22.22)
That Guha, the exceedingly great and most illustrious commander-in-chief of the gods, renowned throughout the worlds—
O Sovereign of the universe, that prince is truly a source of supreme affection for you.

Victorious is Umā, the beloved of the enemy of Tripura and the mother of Gaṇapati and the other Maruts; she who gave birth to the commander of the celestial host for the sake of destroying the enemies of the gods.
May the beloved daughter of the Lord of Mountains attend with a gracious mind to these verses concerning her own family, which speak of her separation from Gaṇanātha.
Miscellaneous (composed in the Naramanoramā meter):
In this chapter, the twenty-four syllables of the *tatsavitur* Gāyatrī mantra are sequentially [arranged] into verses.
In the fourth syllable of the third foot, [the following] is seen:
"Showering nectar as it were with a garland of rays, victorious is that white smile of Śiva’s consort. (23.1)
May your supreme state, ever blooming with joy, manifest within the cave of my heart. 23.2
O queen of the abode of the enemy of Madana, your foot is indeed not different from a lotus. 23.3
The two Śivas, having assumed manifold manifestations through their sovereign powers, brought forth this triple world.
But for you, O beloved of Giriśa, the egg of the lotus-born Brahmā becomes a mere ball for your play.
O Umā, O bestower of true fearlessness, everything exists within your hand; in the Supreme Man, however, nothing at all exists.
How could she, who has earrings of gold and moon, and whose neck is radiant with a garland of stars, not be described? 23.7
Speak constantly of Umā, who possesses manifold virtues; O you of stainless speech, grant me freedom from fear.
Or rather, abandon me;
for I surely worship your feet, O Lord of the World, every single day.
May the wife of the one whose banner bears the bull be one who kisses the lotus-head of Gaṇapati. 23.10.
O Supreme Deity, you lead the people who perform the immersion of the young [image] to your own abode.
O Mother, let this be known by the wise;
yet for the virtuous, your experience is through compassion.
Searching within the heart with an unshakable mind;
purifying the city beloved by the bull-bannered Lord and his horse. || 23.13 ||
O Earth, protectress of the wise, I do not abandon either your lotus-feet or my own.
O Mother, O Supreme Deity, those with grey-haired heads search for these two feet of yours within their hearts.
You yourself are the stainless sustainer of all;
O Mother, you abide in your own majesty.
Finding no stability in Your lotus feet, they revile Brahmā, whose own lotuses lack such splendor.
May my state of distress become the state of Śiva’s consort,
which the sages know as the abode of the three worlds.
O Śivā, by praising your multitude of virtues,
I have become free from fear and have attained a new, unsurpassed joy.
O Mother, by the power of your compassion, this very liberation has occurred for us within the Imperishable, since we have taken refuge at your feet.
O you who are praised by the immortals, that which lies between the eye and its object— that indeed is your supreme body.
"Where indeed does the memory of 'I' shine forth?"—by thus questioning, one dissolves into the Great. 23.22.
O Mother, in your abode, which is known as the nectar, whose nature is bliss and consciousness, and which is sought after by the wise; 23.23.
O source of joy, your foot is touched by my sighing breath,
which is constantly gazing upon it.
May these verses of the true poet Gaṇapati, which are so pleasing to men, bestow joy upon the mountains.
May the smile of Caṇḍikā, white as moonlight, shine upon the earth for the prosperity of the virtuous. (In the *Supratiṣṭhā* meter). 24.1.
May there be for me some wealth for my eyes, which are the eyes of the world, that increases what is auspicious. 24.2.
She brings security to the lineage of the virtuous;
she destroys the hosts of terrible dānavas.
She moves within the true mind joined with yoga;
she is the wise deliverer for those who serve at her feet. || 24.4 ||
May she who captivates the eyes of the Conqueror with flower-arrows,
and who sustains the wheel of the world, protect me.
The śārikā bird born from the twelve-finger space is the single verse of all speech.
She is Svacchamastakā among those who perform meritorious deeds; she is Chinnamastakā among those established in yoga.
Established in the Self, she is the traditional lineage and the promoter of all living beings. || 24.8 ||
May she whose sandals are worthy of worship by the virtuous, and who is the life-partner of Him whose eye is on His forehead, purify me.
From generosity comes fame; from prowess, delight; from wealth, pride; and from virtue, forbearance.
From truth comes dignity in this world;
from sacrifice comes a radiant station in heaven. 24.11
From self-restraint comes freedom from the multitude of sins;
from yoga comes the possession of great spiritual powers.
O Śarvanārī, through the supreme service of your feet, there is the attainment of all excellent fruits.
That supreme accomplishment which is attained through effort is [attained] by one who is beheld by Viśvanāyikā.
O Śivā, you are the mistress of prosperity, of wealth, and of speech; you are the sovereign of the vital breaths and of consciousness.
O Goddess, by means of the eye fixed upon the target of the sky, your meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) is as if perfected.
O Goddess, by placing the nectar (āśira) all around the wind, the sage obtains strength from you. 24.17.
That purification which occurs within the inner chamber of the heart— O Savitṛ, let that be your worship.
O Mother of the World, your cultivation of form is some indescribable mental state that exists even without an object of perception.
One person proclaimed her as an ornament through learning,
while another declared her to be its destruction.
O Mother, by this [speech] you are surpassed by yourself—
by that single, distinct form of intellect.
In the external view, she is the mire of the universe;
otherwise, O Mother, she is absolute existence alone.
To those who possess wealth, you appear like a fragment;
to yogis whose minds are undivided, you are something quite other.
This is bondage that you appear as fragmented; this is liberation that you appear as unfragmented.
O Consort of the Lord, may this well-established and excellent song be for the delight of your heart. 24.25.
The Kṣetramālā (in the Indravajrā meter): Kanyākumārī is exceedingly generous, worthy of honor by all, and non-different from Prakṛti.
May it provoke laughter at the bubbles of the ocean for the happiness of the world. || 25.1 ||
Guard your own mind against intoxication, envy, and the like; beg for food at the proper time for the sake of sustaining the body.
Behold the lotus feet of the Consort of Rāmeśvara if you have a longing for the attainment of liberation.
O friend, if you have fear, [seek] that which has removed the sorrow of its devotees from the world— the ripening of the merit of the glance of the Lord of Hālāsya, which is purifying.
A particular light, with eyes like those of a water-dweller.

He who beholds that sovereign lady of the entire cosmic egg, the supreme Mother who is the power of the living-liṅga, skilled in the method of destroying ignorance—he shall never again obtain a body within this world of existence. 25.4
Who, even if they possessed a thousand mouths, would be able to describe the virtues of the one whose abode is the lotus,
wherein the very birth of all beings takes place?
For liberation, which is difficult even for sages to attain.
May the eye-path of Śiva— who is worshipped by Vyāghrāṅghri and Vātāśana, and who is the hero of the stage of dance— along with his consort Śivakāmā,
be for your [welfare].
May my friends be fruitful in their desires. || 25.6 ||
O Mother Apitakucā, whoever gazes upon you with a restless heart at Aruṇācala—you whose face is like the full moon—becomes possessed of detachment, and all his desires come under his control. (25.7)
He who beholds the capital city of Kuṇḍalīpaṭṭaṇa as something severed at the head—
devoid of essence and lacking any talk of bliss— renounces this saṃsāra through his wisdom.
He who, upon seeing the bride of the Lord of the City of Ādi, dispels the aversion of her eyes— his inner being has shaken off all attachment.
Furthermore, it obstructs the desire for existence. || 25.9 ||
O Lord of Ascetics, may the girdle of the lovely city of Kāñcī, the holy city of the earth, produce an indescribable joy for the householder with the tinkling of its small bells.
May Ambikā nourish you with her glances. || 25.10 ||
They say that beholding the sacred site of Śrī Kālahasti is a repetition of seeing Mount Kailāsa,
for it bestows knowledge upon those who take refuge at its feet.
Where Jñānāmbikā has received her initiation.
By beholding the peak of Śrīśaila, a man shall become free from worldly attachment;
for there resides the abode of her whose curls are like bees.
That [face] of Ambikā, whose confusion has been stilled, is like a bee.
O best of the wise, if you have the mind to attain auspicious intellect and the fulfillment of all desires, look toward Gokarṇagā Bhadrakarṇī on the shore of the western ocean. (25.13)
He who, being dispassionate, beholds the supreme Goddess— who has established her presence there at the famous abode named Karavīra and who is known by the name Puṇyā— [attains liberation].
He is capable of taking the hand of liberation. || 25.14 ||
O friend, if you have any firm desire for knowledge, do not waste this time in vain;
worship the Goddess who resides at Tulajāpura.
Indeed, this [emptiness] is not at all other than its own nature.
Worship that playful companion of the Lord of the World, who assumes the guise of a cowherd girl;
that which is desired and dwells in your heart shall come into your hands.
And the suffering of existence in saṃsāra shall not occur again. || 25.16 ||
By whomsoever this Mother, named Virajā, residing on the banks of the Vaitaraṇī, is propitiated,
by him all else is propitiated.
This essence of the earth is sung by the noble ones. || 25.17 ||
On the bank of the river Sarasvatī, there is a place where throngs of noble ones sing its praises;
he who beholds Kālikā, the dark-haired goddess, there has no fear even of Time itself. (25.18)
She whose abode of divine play is said to be the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas)—
she is Bhadrā, a certain supreme secret mudrā.
She is Kāmeśvarī, the root of the world. 25.19.
Having become the performer of the auspicious sight of Gaurī’s feet, and the upholder of meritorious deeds,
one attains that foremost state which is accessible through those purified by right conduct.
One should attain that state from which there is no fall. || 25.20 ||
Vārāṇasī is truly a sacred field, unsurpassed even throughout the three worlds;
for the sake of its subjects, it holds forth vessels of food.
Where Gaurī herself, the large-eyed one, resides. || 25.21 ||
Having beheld this Nandā, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the gods, whose face is like the moon,
and who dwells upon the Vindhya mountain...
One should not contemplate the terrors of saṃsāra.
A man here who desires to embrace that woman known as liberation, whose body is bliss,
should choose the messenger of the Lord of the Pramathas.
That beloved lady, the mistress of the city of Avanti. || 25.23 ||
I remember that mountain, praised by Siddhas and celestial rishis, where I used to play repeatedly with my brother in the forests.
[He went] to Kailāsa, the mountain that is the mother’s dwelling.
May Gaurī, who sportively dwells upon the white peak of Agastya while the full moon reigns in the sky,
and whose power is hidden within sacred fields such as Kāśī and Indra-vajrā stones, be present here.
This Mother Apītakucā, constantly bringing about awakening for the night-lotuses of the minds of those learned in the Āgamas—
May the moon of laughter, which is a portion of the face of Maheśvara’s consort, protect all the Kula lineages. 26.1.
Her ears kissed by her long eyes,
her fame for charity surpassing the clouds,
she possesses a beloved complexion like that of the Lord of the Crimson Mountain (Śiva).
May Aparṇā destroy the suffering of the world.
The fortune of the eyes of the four Vedas,
sought even by the collections of the Upanishads,
whose face is like the moon that dispels sorrow and scatters nectar—
The secret was beheld on Mount Śoṇa. || 26.3 ||
Cast aside today all doubt regarding the attainment of every desire, which is as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand;
for the daughter of the Mountain King has come within the range of your vision.
Therefore, from this point forward, I am the inner king.
The image of one who knows the arts, entering [the heart] of those with little knowledge, shines forth to enable their crossing;
it has now been obtained upon the mountain of the crimson earth.
Ah! After such a long time, this very woman is my mother.
In this vast circle of the land of Bhārata,
may there be many faultless homes; [may] the orb of the moon, whose splendor is surpassed by [their] faces, [shine therein].
My mother delights here on Mount Śoṇa.
She whose net of sins is washed away by her reliance on the Vāri river, who possesses the unrestrained play of ocean waves,
and whose eyes mimic the petals of a lotus.
Together with her sons, [she was carried away] by the mouth of the king of elephants.
With long, curved, thick, and black hair,
she is the mistress of the heart of the enemy of the water-born arrow; this supreme lady possesses a fame as pure as the flower of the kāśa reed.
May you, whose ornament is the moon, be the breaker of bonds.
Her feet are worshipped by the one born from the lotus; her name is purifying and destroys the mud [of sin];
she is the supreme wish-fulfilling vine for her servants.
The nectar from the eye of Śaṅkara is our refuge. || 26.9 ||
This golden-wombed mouth, praised by the *jhillī* of the bow of the five-arrowed god, with its flickering eyes like bending celestial creepers, is here.
The five-faced goddess is our refuge. || 26.10 ||
O Mother, having shaken off the soldiers of passion and the like by means of the terrifying sound of his anklets,
alas, he has forcibly stolen my heart!
O dweller at the feet of Śoṇanaga, [I bow to] your foot. || 26.11 ||
O simple one, place my words in your ear; abandon attachment to wealth and the like,
and cultivate devotion at the feet of the Queen of the Lord of Crimson Mountains.
Practice, practice, and you shall attain liberation.
When the entire body has become exceedingly worn by old age, and delusion robs one of the strength of the intellect— alas, O Mother, at the end, the mind becomes scorched by the heat of suffering.
He does not wish to serve your feet. || 26.13 ||
Those who know the Tantras maintain that the ninefold womb is a wheel with the form of a red lip;
half of this body belongs to the Enemy of Madana, and the other half is your own limb, O Daughter of the Mountain King.
O daughter of the Lord of Mountains, let this linga here also be composed of fire; for even one who is free from the qualities (guṇas) cannot exist without union with you.
O Goddess, from where indeed does the splendor of Śiva arise? 26.15
O Sovereign of the World, this beautiful image of yours, established for worship, is worthy of salutation;
this form of yours is the very half of the Crimson Mountain.
To proclaim [the glory] of the Daughter of the Mountain, who has shaken off all sin.
O you whose body is half that of the Crimson Mountain (Śoṇanaga), you constantly hold Guha, known as Ramaṇa, upon your lap;
yet, alas, why do you repeatedly drive away Gaṇapa, even though he has arrived? 26.17.
To Guha, who dwells upon the hip and wears the guise of a human youth, she yielded much milk to be given as a gift to her lover, whose body was half that of the Crimson Mountain.
O Mother, you shine here with your yellow garment.
O Mother Pītamapītakucā, you sleep by the power of your perfect meditative absorption; you do not perceive your son, your lover, who dwells upon your lap.
Having gazed as much as desired upon the milk from her broad breasts.
O Mother, having drunk that breast-milk called the essence of knowledge, this Rāma, the sovereign of sages,
became entirely composed of wisdom, O Goddess.
For by that [food] the self indeed nourishes the body. || 26.20 ||
O Pārvatī, O Śivā, may much of the milk from the jar-like breasts— which has not been drunk by the wise Guha— be given for the sake of joy.
O Sovereign, bestow upon me even a small portion [of this]. || 26.21 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, if you know this mature son of yours to be bearing the water of rut, then let there be no milk;
bestow instead sinless food.
By which I may hold power, O Maheśvarī. || 26.22 ||
O Mother, if all that I have earned by my own effort is to be enjoyed by me alone, then grant me, O Lady,
the most excellent of blessings.
Send forth those victorious ones to the earth.
With playful glances flashing like lightning, her secret intentions revealed in the act of looking,
she possesses a face like the full moon and limbs of exquisite grace.
The companion of the fiery liṅga is our refuge. || 26.24 ||
O Mother, O Pītakucā, O Consort of the Lord of Aruṇaśaila, O You who are to be honored by the sun—
Gaṇanātha, having composed it well, offers this garland of Dodhaka verses unto You.

Dispersing darkness in every direction, warding off unrighteousness, spreading prosperity, and instantly pacifying the mass of suffering; generating an incomparable fluid within the thousand-petaled lotus of my heart—the slight trace of the white smile of the fierce Caṇḍī triumphs. (Śikhariṇī metre) 27.1.
Resembling a blazing forest fire upon the heads of enemies,
yet comparable to the orb of the nectar-rayed moon upon the heads of those who are humble;
it robs the darkness of adversaries of its power, like the rising sun.
May the foot of Pracaṇḍā Caṇḍī destroy the prosperity of the wicked.
I worship the abode of speech, the birthplace of all intellects, the source of all powers, the beloved of the Lord of the entire universe;
she whom the lotus-eyed women of Hayagrīva worship with heart-stealing songs, as sweet as the warbling of female cuckoos at the onset of spring.

O crusher of Mahiṣa, that body of yours which blazes with splendors; O consort of Giriśa, that body of yours which shines with loveliness—apart from anger and love, there was no distinction whatsoever between the two. The former is Durgā, and the other is Lalitā, as praised by the sage.
There are a thousand suns belonging to the Lord of the Days;
there are a thousand heads belonging to the Lord of the Serpents;
there are a thousand eyes belonging to the Lord of the Gods.
At that time, O Haimavatī, you possess a thousand arms.
The moon of his face is serene, there is no redness at all in his eyes,
no trembling in his bimba-red lips, and even his smile is as bright as a blooming kāśa flower; his lotus-like hand is free from calluses and exceedingly tender.
O Mother, that blazing trident was indeed terrifying to Śumbha.
O Mother, whatever form you assumed during the slaying of Śumbha— bearing supreme powers and a luster comparable to the essence of moonbeams—
by meditating upon that form again and again, O friend of the Destroyer of Smara, this agitated mind of mine finds rest, O you who are like a wish-fulfilling creeper for those who worship you.
O Savitrī, if you are skilled in the destruction of the three worlds, then I entreat you, who are praised as being born from the interior of a lotus:
O Blessed One, these various sins of mine roar out; therefore, display against them that renowned and most terrifying power of yours.

O Mother, who delights in the arena of battle, you bestowed the *śakti* upon this man, the eye of the worlds, who took the form of Narasiṃha; he who, out of wrath, tore open the chest of Kanakakaśipu with his exceedingly sharp-pointed claws, which were licked by the breasts of the Daughter of the Ocean.

He conquered that thousand-spoked wheel, which had manifested its banner throughout the three worlds, which was the lord of the serpents with a mouth like a row [of teeth], who had become familiar with the prison of Yama,
and who had visibly assumed a human body.
O Ambā, through your very possession, the young son of the twice-born has become a supreme axe to his beloved.
That power of yours, which remains tireless even at the end of the entire universe,
formerly abandoned the enemy of kings at the conclusion of its task and entered the descendant of Kakutstha for the purpose of destroying the lineage of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
Having abandoned the thousand-rayed sun as the day wanes, she shines like the moon.
When the multitude of worlds has been rescued by you alone, O Blessed One, that slayer of the cities (Śiva), possessed of fourfold intelligence, approaches at the proper time to acquire fame;
and when the protection of the world has been accomplished by you, O Mother, Viṣṇu also meets him from somewhere to obtain glory through the slaughter of the Rākṣasa—how indeed is he not skillful?

Your own nature is the thunderbolt; in the sky, you have as your limiting adjunct the subtle light of the cosmic dust-particles. Your hymn of praise becomes a certain flickering, slender radiance. Your pervasiveness is unobstructed, and all strength has been granted to you, O Treasure of Power. You prevail over yourself by a thousandfold portion and over everything else, O Auspicious One.
Since you cook the world under the guise of Time through the power of your lightning-like radiance, the best of the wise know you as Kālī;
and since, having become the weapon of the Lord, you burn his enemies with your vajra-form, O Goddess of inexhaustible strength, they call you the fierce Caṇḍī.

"O Unaging One, one sage calls you Indra; yet another seer who knows the truth says that he is Indra, rich in weapons, [and that you are Śrī]. You two, O Blessed Lady, are mother and son and are not to be distinguished; therefore, among the assemblies of the wise, the destinies of the intelligent are twofold. (27.15)
Manifesting the universe through various distinctions of qualities, transforming and shaking all states of being to obstruct the course of the world, and spreading forth the entire universe—
both moving and unmoving— to protect you, O Śarva, a certain [power] acts.
Investigating even the slightest fragment of a person's actions, the Lords prevail.
Just as the radiance of the sun becomes the fierce power that heats the entire world, so you are the power of the Lord of all worlds who blazes;
like the moonlight of the nectar-rayed moon, you gladden the heart of one who enters [his presence].
The waves of joy arising from the elements and so forth become the small cavity [of the heart].
Are you Pracaṇḍā or Gaurī? Among the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, he is Bhīma or Śambhu, the all-pervading bestower of fearlessness to those who take refuge at his feet.
One form of these two sports together with the Lord in this vast sky; the other plays in the supreme, white light.

O Mother Īśānī, you who are divided twofold in the sky like the cool-rayed moon, and likewise manifest in two beautiful forms—the blazing orb and the lovely female body—tell me, which of these two was my place of birth in a former life? Was I born from the fierce one, or indeed from the formidable one?

Due to the difference in the eyes, no distinction whatsoever arises in the vision; nor does a difference arise in the hands due to their separation, for they become one through the unity of the celestial palace (*abhivimāna*).
Thus, even though there is a difference between the two bodies, O Śivā, it does not lead to a division within You, whether You are Caṇḍī in the region of the sky or Gaurī in the white light.
When the head of the human being was severed by the earth-knower who understands all the scriptures,
and when [the skull] had been split open through abundant austerity,
you became free from contact with the body and the senses within the *suṣumnā* channel.
Endowed with external power and having shaken off long sleep, you shine forth.

Or rather, when the head was severed from the slender-limbed daughter of the Bhrigu lineage by the command of her father, did you not place your own formidable, vast, and sinless splendor— O lotus-eyed one trembling with fear— within me?
Then they said to you, O Mother of celebrated deeds: "Your head has been cut off."
O Blessed Mother, when you entered the ascetic’s body— the sacrificial fire made flickering and matted with streams of blazing flames— then,
from her severed head, blood flowed profusely from her throat.
Through Kabandha, an indescribable greatness, revered by the world, was attained.
O Blessed One, I feel no shame in stealing from you, the treasure-house, as I create upon this earth poetic speech that partakes in the fragrance of your stainless fame;
and in performing my dance of devotion, I carry away the multitude of flowers from the garden of the king.
Spreading it out for him and repeatedly offering it up, like a servant. || 27.24 ||

May the mountain peaks of Gaṇapati shine in this world— peaks that instill supreme contentment in the minds of great poets, bestow a fresh and noble sentiment upon the assembly of the learned, and instantly inspire the families devoted to the consort of Śiva.
Description of Reṇukā and others (in the Vasantatilakā meter): Causing the illusion of a pale inner halo around the full orb of her moon-like face, [the dust of the forest]...
May the smile of the Lord of the Pramathas, whose lotus-like eyes are those of the women of the inner apartments, grant you supreme joy. 28.1.
They are the delusions of the moon, the revivers of the lotus-arrowed god,
and the inflammers of the power of Śakti among those who bow before her.
May my smiles be auspicious and full of joy. || 28.2 ||
May some Mother with severed head take away my sins— she who bestows joy upon the servants of her lotus feet,
and who remains sleepless in the act of granting boons to her devoted people.
He makes his dwelling on the sandy banks of the Kamaṇḍaludhunī river. || 28.3 ||
May that unique heroine, the terrifying mother who gave birth to the sixth incarnation and who is ever-vigilant in the act of protecting her devotees, dispel the misfortunes of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
It shines upon the sacred sandy bank of the Kamaṇḍaludhunī river.
If the Sage, free from passion, commanded for the sake of severance,
and if his son, possessed of many virtues, severed his mother—
then the Lord, the Master of all power, [severed] the body that was to be burned.
And if this most wonderful story has entered [your mind].
Your beloved son suddenly severed your head;
yet, filled with joy, you danced—
neither was there any sin on his part, nor any loss whatsoever for you.
Alas, this was the ripening of the deeds of his own arms! || 28.6 ||
That very Surabhi was Ambā, whom King Bhīṣma took by force; and he, in turn, gave her to the descendant of Bhṛgu (Śaradvat).
The cause of his death was precisely his dwelling in another's house.
The story of seeing the Gandharva is merely a fabrication of the enemy. 28.7.
How many heads have not been severed from embodied beings?
Yet, in this world, only the head of Renuka’s son is worshipped.
How many navels have not been cut from those possessing bodies? Yet, only that of Viṣṇu is honored.
The fragrant musk deer, alone, intoxicates the mind.
The vital breaths remain in the body even when it is deprived of the head;
yet his severed head rests playfully like a lotus in his hand.
Thus, the wise understand through their intellect that this entire universe is dependent upon him alone.
Let them behold this wonder in the city of Nandana. || 28.9 ||
May Ambikā, the mistress of Prāṇa, accept the refuge of me who shines in the city of Vidhi;
for by drinking the milk from her jar-like breasts, the sovereign of poets became the very embodiment of their kinship. 28.10
She whose three sons do not cast even a glance of compassion upon the construction of worlds or the felling of forests—
she alone is the sole mother of the universe.
May the supreme auspicious Prakṛti be the destroyer of our sins. || 28.11 ||
She is the full moon for the awakening of the heart,
the boat for people falling into the ocean of calamity,
and the graceful three-colored banner of the Vedas' standard.
May some commentary on the root text of Śiva be my refuge.

May that wife of the Lord of Beings protect us— she whose head is graced by a multitude of flowers like a noble man honored in an assembly, and who, as the ground for his feet, receives the foremost seat.
This darkness envelops me on all sides— not only myself, but my family and my country as well; yet,
quickly, upon the peak of the mountain of my own heart’s rising, it shall vanish.
May the glorious one, who possesses a garland of rays from his feet, arise for you.

May the lotus-foot of the Daughter of the Mountain—beautiful with the luster of the friend of the fresh lotus (the sun), its qualities enhanced by the radiance of the jewels in the crowns of the gods headed by Brahmā—dispel my suffering. 28.15.
May the twangs of the bowstring of Kāma, who desires to conquer Giriśa in battle— twangs that serve as invitations to a flock of swans—
dispel the misfortune of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Those were the tinklings from the anklets on her lotus-like feet.
I bow to that foot of the Great Radiance, which assumes both female and male forms, who conquered Mahiṣa— the crusher of all worlds— and whose very deed was the subduing of Antaka (Death) himself.
I go for refuge to him whose voice is sweet with the sound of anklets. || 28.17 ||
O Mother, whose heart is filled with compassion, please uplift this wretched one who has sunk into a mass of most terrible poison and has sought refuge at Your feet.
O lady of the family of Kubera’s friend, this burden belongs to you alone.
O Sovereign of the World, O Mother Mṛḍānī, who art endowed with compassion, lift up me who have fallen into the blind well of calamity, my vision obstructed on all sides by masses of darkness!
[He touched] his son with a hand that grants fearlessness to the worlds.

O Mistress of my life, for this servant of your lotus feet— whose manliness has been rendered fruitless by the ripening of misfortune— tell me the means [to attain you], O Sovereign of the world of the Pramathas.
Look upon yourself alone as one skilled in the method of delivering others.
Seated upon the edge of the jeweled throne of Mṛtyuñjaya’s thighs, her cheeks enhanced by the brilliance of her earrings,
with the lotuses of her hands shining with ruby bracelets—
O you who have been born from the Lord of the Kulācala mountains, destroy our sin!
O Mother, is your body fair as refined gold?
O Enchantress of the Foe of Kama, is it as white as a digit of the moon? Or is its luster as dark as a ripe sapphire?
Or I remember her, possessing the luster of a bud of the bandhūka flower. || 28.22 ||
You are Sundarī; you are the Mother Dhūmāvatī who has conquered the race of kings; you are Ajare, the Sovereign of the World;
you are Kālī; O Īśvarī, you are she who holds the young parrot.
O Tārā, you are the edge of a sword that shatters the calamities of those who have taken refuge in you.
You are the divine Bhairavī, you are Bagalāmukhī,
and you are Rāmā who wanders through the lotus groves;
you are the streak of the nectar-rayed moon to the eyes of the dweller of Kailāsa.
Who knows, O Mother, the glories of those who possess birth?

May these verses in the Vasantatilakā meter by the lord of poets, which have captivated the heart of the youthful conqueror of cities through his abundant compassion, shake off all calamities for those who love virtuous deeds and scatter all misfortunes upon those who long for sin. 28.25.
The ninefold homage (*madalekhāvṛtta*):
May the slight smiles of Pārvatī—the life-sustainer of the worlds and the delight of the eyes of the Enemy of Tripura—bring us great joy. (29.1)
Days should not be spent pointlessly at excessive expense;
rather, the faultless deeds of one's mother should be heard.
Exert yourself, O tongue, to destroy misfortunes;
let the purifying deeds of the Daughter of the Mountain be celebrated.
Attachment to worldly prosperity must be warded off, and no anxiety whatsoever should be entertained;
rather, the noble refuge of the destitute should be constantly held in the mind. 29.4
That internal power which exists for knowing, speaking, hearing, breathing, or seeing—abide here; this is mindfulness. (29.5)
One should meditate upon the form of the Mother of the World, which possesses the splendor of hundreds of suns, bears the moon upon her head, and purifies all sins.
For those whose hearts are tormented by the weight of their sin,
service at the feet of Rudrāṇī is the expiation.
I serve those two radiant feet where there are ten toes that are like hundreds of suns.
If you do not become angry when I ask for something, or if you remain silent after my request, then accept my service, O Mother; do what you wish, or do not.
This footstool for the worship of Śarvāṇī’s feet shall be a place of execution for formidable misfortunes.
If this strength has been obtained by touching the footstool of the Mother of Skanda,
then each single [particle] would be equal to a great sin, and each single [particle] would be like a thunderbolt.
We bow down to the lotus-like foot of Śambhu’s principal queen, in order to destroy the fierce accumulation of our sins. 29.12
For those who bow down to the lotus-like feet of Kālī, nothing remains impossible;
my word is never false.
Your stay here is finished; O Paṅketu, go far away!
At this time, we pay our respects to Kālī, the consort of Śaṅkara.
O Hope, such is your condition as you dance upon the surface of the earth!
Where indeed is the end of desires? Bow down to the Enemy of Desire (Śiva), not to women.
Blessed are those who bow before the daughter of the snowy mountain;
I consider all others with uplifted heads to be merely wild buffaloes.
The wise, bowing down to the lotus feet of Umā,
receive within themselves a radiant splendor through her own power.
The two givers—the Mandara tree and the feet of the Daughter of the Mountain—are equal;
yet the fruit from the former is obtained by those with upraised necks, while that from the latter is obtained by those with bowed necks.
I am this very one, a servant of Śarvāṇī, the conqueror even of Time,
and a sovereign of the world of poets.
Show passion toward the red lotus-feet of Rudrāṇī; thus the mind cultivates beauty in the presence of that which possesses the essence of all essences. 29.20.
Having thoroughly examined the web of scriptural traditions, we shall proclaim the essential meaning:
devotion to the feet of Skanda’s Mother leads both to worldly enjoyment and to liberation.
Compassion for those who have no refuge is the life-force of merit;
friendship with many is the foremost cause of prosperity in this world. (29.22)
Love for one's own wife fulfills a praiseworthy desire;
devotion to the feet of Śarvāṇī fulfills the eternal desire. (29.23)
Thus, although it is one, it becomes manifold through the diversity of its objects; this internal melting called *rati* produces various distinctions of fruit.
May this Heramba, spreading a certain joy for his mother through a weight of devotion, bestow lines of rut-fluid.
May she who is born of the snowy mountain grant me auspiciousness through her smile, which is naturally white, held eternally in her face, and performed with the mind. (In the Pramāṇikā meter) 30.1.
Relinquishing sense-objects that perish at every moment,
I worship the Sovereign Goddess who dwells within the universe, having discerned her with my mind.
Or, O Mother, when my heart is held by you like a pure mirror,
grant your presence within your own body, which is without a self, O daughter of the mountain.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, may that white lotus situated in the center of the city serve as your seat, which is the foundation of the cosmic egg.
O Mother, beloved of the one who wears the new moon as his crest-jewel, may your feet—which flow with an unbroken stream—sustain the life of my devotion; may they be honored with water for the feet.
O Mother, Sovereign of all, may this water from the lake of my mind—whose current is the washing away of latent impressions—be an invaluable offering for your hands. 30.6.
O beloved of Bhava, by contemplating Mahendra-yoni,
may you drink this great nectar for the sake of purification.
With the nectar-water flowing from the thousand-petaled lotus,
she who possesses thousand-petaled eyes is consecrated by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
O fair-limbed mother, whatever pleasure has been earned by my five senses, that is offered to you; may it become for you the fivefold nectar known as *sudhā*.
O Śivā, let this very body of mine, fashioned by a twice-born man born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, become a divine garment for you.
May this body of mine, bearing various fine threads,
serve as your sacrificial thread (*upavīta*) for the sake of a form easily awakened by bliss.
O Śivā, may this fragrance of the mind, born from my own realization of reality as I search for the Great One, be for you like sandalwood.
May this breath of life, which now exhales as the sigh of Maheśanārī,
become for me a constant worshiper of you.
O Mother, may this [offering] of mine be for you: a guggulu resin of merit, blazing with the fire of the time of ripening, bearing the incense-stick of excellent perfumes.
O Goddess, this Lamp of Awakening, which bestows supreme joy, has been kindled by me, a silent sage who has entered the cave; may it be for your delight. 30.15.
I offer this most beloved and intensely flavorful egoity; O You who are free from affliction, let it be consumed by You.
Sarasvatī acts as nectar and bestows a state of fullness upon the mind;
O Mother, these three, having come together, are offered to you like a leaf held within the heart.
May the lightning-creeper, its form shining amidst the dark-blue clouds, be your own manifesting power. 30.18.
O Ambikā, this sound, like a bee, then took refuge in that sound;
O Goddess, having consecrated me, it bestows wisdom upon your feet.
Since I am here to perform your worship without interruption,
O Consort of Viśvanātha, no ritual dismissal (visarjana) is prescribed for you.
O Mother, O Mistress of the Universe, there is no separation here from the one who bears the moon;
he shines right here within the tip of the flash of lightning.
Having contemplated this body as a solitary new temple, O Bhavānī, you who possess the Lord should perform your divine play within it.
O Queen of the palace of my heart, there is no purpose for sleep as there is for the dull-witted or the indolent; you are entreated only that you may sport here.
This, your eldest son, has taken recourse to a human form; O Mṛḍānī, behold what kind of excellence this abode of his body possesses! 30.24
May this *Pramāṇikāvalī* by the great poet Gaṇeśitṛ be sounded within the lotus of the mind during the worship of Maheśvarī. (30.25)
The Glory of the Name (in the Upajāti meter):
May the river born from the mountain [Gaṅgā], whose beauty is feigned by her gentle smile, wash away all the mud clinging to my heart as it sinks in the cycle of existence. 31.1.
Having united with the loud laughter of Hara like a son with his father or a disciple with his teacher,
may he, shining brilliantly, grant me auspiciousness.
The sprout of laughter of her who has the lion as her vehicle. || 31.2 ||
Salutations to Śivā, who bestows supreme intellect upon you bipeds;
salutations to Ambikā, the sovereign of the Ādhāra-cakra.
To the creator of the wheel of the universe. || 31.3 ||
Even cows low at specific times; is he not a man who does not call out "Mother"?
Furthermore, let everything be observed as possessing life-force, for within everyone there exists a supreme power.
Having fixed your aim upon yourself or elsewhere— that primordial power which is dormant within all things—
invoke it repeatedly until its awakening.
If she awakens, what indeed would be impossible? || 31.5 ||
Those who, bearing supreme peace,
dwell in solitude while chanting the names of the Daughter of the Cool-Mountain;
They are victorious even over your father, Jayanta.

For those people who proclaim the names of the compassionate Mother of the Elephant-Faced One, it is false to say that they experience exhaustion from dwelling again within the womb of their own mother. 31.7.
O wise one, even though I am assailed on all sides by evils, I place my trust in your prowess,
provided that you do not speak as one who knows the taste [of fear].
I have been struck down by the names of the moon-bearer.
O Auspicious One, O Mother of the World, O Durgā! You raise the cry of "Give! at the gates of others who are arrogant with the pride of their abundant wealth.
"Protect me!"—why does this not come, O Mother Tongue? 31.9
O connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, if you have a profound passion for uttering sentences radiant with rasa,
why not let them end with "namas," which scatters nectar?
We have no names for the mother of the prince. || 31.10 ||
That which is sung as the name of the Daughter of the Mountain is itself to be understood as the primary meritorious deed;
so they say for the sake of the ignorant world.
The wise know that merits such as sacrifices are supreme.

By the Sāman properly employed, the world may be brought under control; by the Nāman constantly recited, one becomes the leader of the world. He who has mastered both of these correctly is truly accomplished.
For him, there shall be no fear from anything whatsoever in this world. || 31.12 ||
Śarva’s consort is pleased by the chanting [of her name],
yet once pleased, she does not grant one's desired object; for she does not know this means in the world.
Human beings go to states of woe in many ways. || 31.13 ||
Abandoning all other desires, he spoke the names of her who is beloved by the serpent-ornamented one (Śiva),
even though her deeds transcend the world and are most terrible.
What can he do to me, the offspring of the Sun? || 31.14 ||
He who desires to attain perfection through sacrifice, gifts, or rigorous vows,
would be like one lying on his mother’s lap seeking to grasp the moon.
For one who recites the name of Maheśvarī, there is success.
Having thoroughly analyzed the secret tantras and cast far away all pretense, I proclaim the essence:
it is simply the name of the consort of the Enemy of Kāma.
The cause of success is neither sacrifice nor charity. || 31.16 ||
Those who are eager to drink from the lips of Rāma call nectar only slightly sweet;
they are rather eager for the fire of the arrow named Kāmāri-Rāma.
The lords of poets speak of sour gruel.
The lower lip of young women is some indescribable vessel of nectar; the poet is to be called a cloud of nectar-water;
this [poem] is a canopy of spreading waves of nectar.
The cry of the name of the mountain maiden.
In the abode of the gods, nectar alone shines most brightly;
in the speech of great poets, it is another kind of nectar; and upon the bimba-like lips of lotus-eyed women, there is yet another nectar.
The two names of the Mother of the World are difficult to comprehend. || 31.19 ||
Sweetness shines in the lips of young women; clarity resides in the orb of the moon, the friend of the cakora bird;
and purity dwells in the waters of the triple-streamed river.
And there is also a triad in the name of Tripurāmbikā. || 31.20 ||
That sweetness which awakens when the beloved’s fine cloth is bitten by one filled with passion is seen here in a song through the weight of devotion.
In that which is named after the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.

That the lips of the daughter of the mountain, though they belong to one who is greedy for the world, possess such colors—that is what I call her nectar; for you describe those lips of hers as consisting of nectar, whereas mine consist of saliva.
O tongue, utter again and again the names of the Mother of the World, which cast away all sins;
we shall speak them only when they are as pleasing to you as groves of honey-sweet mangoes and plantains.
The unbearable dispute concerning the lips of a beloved woman surpasses the excellence of sugarcane and proclaims on all sides the defects of nectar.
The sound of the name of the one who wears matted hair as his final covering. || 31.24 ||
May the majesty of the Mountain Maiden’s name— so utterly incomprehensible to those devoid of faith,
yet sung even by the Siddhas— be victorious!
These Upajāti verses sing to us. 31.25.
May devotion and yoga bestow prosperity upon me—
[that devotion] which is like moonlight captivating the eyes of the Lord of the entire world.
A certain moon of laughter, cool and dispelling darkness, was born to his mother, though devoid of limbs. || 32.1 ||
Her heart moistened by the essence of compassion, smiling with the clear waves of emotion surging from within her heart—
she is the beloved of the Lord of the Pramathas.
May it be for the welfare of the servant at his feet. 32.2.
O Mother, that twofold form of yours which was proclaimed by the sages due to the distinction between cause and effect—
one of those is to be sustained by this [world].
But for the sake of sport, O beloved of the Lord of Beings, there is something else.
To hear this particular hymn,
to understand that such a devotee is of such a nature,
and to grant the desired object—
O mother, your form becomes that of the world of the moon. || 32.4 ||
O Mother, by the analogy of a young monkey, the yogi bears Your causal form;
by the analogy of a young cat...
You nourish your devotee through the form of action.
O Moonlight of the Eye of Maheśa, if the yogin does not possess firm concentration and does not waver from you,
and if he maintains the thought "this is not mine," then, O Mother, you do not immediately abandon that devotee.
A yogi whose fortitude is lax, being excessively drawn away by external objects,
has his own discernment lost.
O Mother, when devotion is turbid with the expansion of egoism... || 32.7 ||
Devotion accompanied by egoism is not devotion;
steadfastness directed toward external objects is not [true] steadfastness for you, O Sovereign of All.
Those who do not understand this—
The devotee and the yogi would not both achieve perfection. || 32.8 ||
O Mother, that devotee who, above all else, holds your lotus feet dear possesses wondrous power.
O Blessed One, what is there in this world that he does not accomplish? 32.9
Even a desire that has been accomplished becomes curtailed when one is under the sway of the greed for individuality;
it is like reaching the very ocean itself [only to find it diminished].
How much water could a jar hold? || 32.10 ||
O Consort of Śambhu, for that man who attains union with You even while still living,
all desires are fulfilled.
They quickly come under the control of one who is free from various delusions. || 32.11 ||
This personality has been bestowed upon you by my presiding intelligence through the power of enjoyment over a long period of time.
My mother, the body disputes; what shall I do? || 32.12 ||
The subtle intellect is not able to engage in a quarrel with the gross physical body;
therefore, O Mother, since you are exceedingly powerful, take what is yours from it by your own strength.

O Mother, Daughter of the Mountain, because you abide in the hearts of all beings as the very essence of their vital breath, therefore the worship of all living creatures is for you no different from your own direct worship.
Some offer oblations into the fire,
perceiving that from it your attainment comes;
others offer oblations into living beings.
"You are directly the vital breath (prāṇa) existing within them. || 32.15 ||

The yogi who constantly worships that breathless, beginningless, and stainless life-force which resides within the self and exists even within all living beings as the source of all elements; [he attains liberation].
O Mother, through that oblation, satisfaction for you is easily obtained.
O Mother, he who, facing the small space within, offers his vital breaths into the supreme Self—
the Prāṇa which is your own sinless form— [attains liberation].
By him, everything has been conquered in the garden of the Lord’s mind.
O Mother, my gaze— withdrawed from all sense-objects, unwinking, and drawn inward— is offered as an oblation into the vital breath within the heart by means of a firm step upon Your form.
O Goddess, [I hear] that inner, hidden sound called Praṇava, which belongs to your portion, the supreme vital breath, as if it were listening.
O Mother of the World, there itself the hearing of it becomes an oblation offered.
In the primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the Mistress of the Heart of Īśa, all mantras and hymns always resound in a hidden manner.
While you are breathing, the silent one offers speech as an oblation.
If the mind falters within the body, it offers itself as an oblation to the objects of the senses, thereby becoming identified with those objects;
yet if it turns back from the body...
When offered into you, who are subtle, it becomes your very form. || 32.21 ||
O Queen of all the worlds, what enjoyment do you not offer to the Blessed One, who makes the experiences of touch, taste, and smell his own through the power of his vital breath?
O Mother, Sovereign of all worlds, he who performs even a single action— whether walking, acting, releasing, or enjoying— is [liberated].
By that [meditation], he performs a constant sacrifice. || 32.23 ||
Among all fires,
the fire of the vital breath (prāṇāgni) has been declared by you to be the most excellent manifestation; indeed,
what is offered into it is a truly well-offered sacrifice.
Substances, cognitions, actions, and the mantra consisting of the syllable Om. || 32.24 ||
May this section, which has surpassed the sweetness of honey and nectar, having emerged from the mouth of Gaṇapati, be for the pleasure of Śarva’s beautiful-eyed consort. 32.25.
The Thirty-third Chapter: Recitation, Yoga, and Offering (in the Vaṃśastha meter).
Shedding nectar that removes all afflictions...
Dispelling the darkness with a mass of radiance and bestowing inexhaustible splendor in every direction,
