the sprouts of the smile of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain are victorious.

O Maheśa, by what deed can your compassionate glance be obtained—by the wife of the pure inner apartments, through the incessant chanting of mantras, by the purification of the intellect, or perhaps by the offering of one's heart? || 33.2 ||
O Goddess, you are won over by the purification of the mind; O Consort of the Lord, you are pleased by the offering of the heart;
through the recitation of the auspicious mantra, you increase.
Within the physical body of the Sustainer of the three worlds. || 33.3 ||
The contemplation of Vedic mantras undoubtedly brings about the increase of mental power;
it is praised for the kindling of the light of the vital breaths.
Endowed with compassion, she is served by the mantras of the Tantras.
O Mother, O golden-limbed one, he who serves your supreme tantric mantra— which transcends all praise—
penetrates the world from which the lightning-like splendor issues forth as if from a wondrous machine.

The mind of one who worships your great mantra, O Mother, does not fall under the sway of mental afflictions; his vision is not dragged away by sense objects; and his body is not ravaged by diseases. (33.6)
O Ambikā, they remember Māyā together with Gaganāgni and Śānti, accompanied by Sacchabhāsā;
likewise, they declare Rasajñā to be with Druhiṇāgni and Śānti, while Dogdhrī is joined with Kha, Ṣa, the sixth vowel, and Bindu.
Today Bhuvaneśvarī was proclaimed by the wise; thereafter, O Mother, Kālikā was spoken of; and the supreme Pracaṇḍacaṇḍī has been celebrated. These three Mantras as well yield great fruit.
The pure ethereal dust, having become a limiting adjunct, directly assumes the state of the Mistress of the World;
resting upon that is the wondrous, all-pervading Power.
A certain high-minded woman was urged by Kālī. || 33.9 ||
She is said to be the sovereign mistress of all heroic exploits— the initiator of those who uphold the empire of the immortals, and the dancer upon the vast stage of the three worlds.
O Mother, this digit of yours is known as Pracaṇḍacaṇḍī.
Remembering the mantra, the devoted sage weeps as he grasps Your feet, O Mother; he clings to them,
yet it is the first one who shall attain the fruit after a long time.
The other finds the nectar at the very first step. || 33.11 ||
O Mother, your foot has been sought by me many times with joy, as if it were touched within my heart;
yet immediately thereafter, out of grief, I flee downward.
I weep for that which is beyond the supreme, by means of the sound of mantras.
The virtuous say, O Mother of the Maruts, that this Great Mantra is the sunlight from your feet;
for from that root has emerged this sound which, consisting of light, blazes forth, consuming the mass of sins.
O Mother, I have repeatedly exerted myself in my search for the root of your birth, while directly upholding the splendor of your feet.
The path which the great seer Ramaṇa proclaimed.
If the referent "I" is the creeper of consciousness,
then how could this [ego] be something other than the milch-cow of experience?
If "I" am the articulated speech of the resonance of the vital breath, [then what else remains]?
It is not possible for Kūrca to say, "I do not know. || 33.15 ||
But that power of consciousness which others maintain, the Tantrikas have called Kuṇḍalinī;
this extraordinary wonder deceives the dull-witted who remain far from the essence of the Āgamas. (33.16)
For those who have attained awakening, there is unbroken experience; for yogis, there is an exceedingly subtle experience.
And all kinds of supernatural powers lie within the reach of one devoted to the mantra of Maheśvarī.
Even thousands of births would be dear to me if you were devoted in birth after birth;
for if the memory of you should fade, there would be no joy.
Even liberation acts for me like a beloved of the Lord. || 33.18 ||
If an object were to exist even without being perceived,
it would not be distinguished from a non-existent thing by that existence which is devoid of its fruit [perception]. But how, indeed, does this "existent" differ from the "non-existent"?
At that time, O dear one, there was no distinction between the liberated soul and a stone.
If liberation is held to be the cessation of sorrows,
and if there is no occurrence of happiness here,
then the intellect does not shine even while that [liberation] exists.
The insentient is distinguished from the liberated by speech alone. || 33.20 ||
The intellect directed outward becomes the cause of worldly transaction; directed inward, it leads to the attainment of the ultimate truth.
He whose mind penetrates both these directions [is truly wise].
And he is considered a perfected one (siddha) by both his feet and his head. || 33.21 ||
He whose mind always possesses a firm footing within,
even while moving externally by means of his intellect,
is proclaimed as one who is immersed in you, O Mother.
For him, there is no fear even as he wanders through the cycle of existence.
In reflection, the wondrous power of thought;
in vision, the radiant power of perception;
and in speech, the supreme power of expression.
One who contemplates you is not conquered by the sense-objects.
As the poet gazes, his vision has abandoned attachment to all that is being beheld;
before his eyes is ever-present Śivā, who is free from fear and praised by the gods.

May this host stationed on the charming bamboo-flute of the Lord of Ganas— purifier of the fears of the virtuous and capable of warding off the entire flood of sins— thoroughly delight the mind of the Great Lord, whose eyes are like lotuses.
Prayer (in the Hariṇī meter):
His greatness is known through his manifold and wondrous acts of sustaining the universe;
his deeds are celebrated for increasing the majesty of the world of Śarva.
May the auspicious smile of Śiva, a treasury of light that reveals his virtues by obstructing the spread of the darkness of evil, grant me blessings. 34.1.
His heart is filled with compassion, his arms with great strength, his lotus-feet with the fortune that provides sustenance for devotees,
and his moon-like face with such beauty that it eclipses the power of the three-eyed Shiva's gaze.
May Kālī, who bestows much, protect me, her devotee at her feet.

If a person recites the mantra of the Goddess, who is praised by the sages, he becomes like an ocean of nectar, purified, and a knower of the various types of separation, having attained perfection through her who is the sovereign of the world, the milch-cow of desires, or the knower of all tastes.
He rains down a stream of words here in this world of the living.
The slender-waisted Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus, having appeared before him and approached his presence with a multitude of horses and elephants, attends upon him;
and this entire universe, along with the gods, once again comes under his control.
And this group of eight also pertains to the accomplishments (siddhis) of those whose fame is renowned.
From the anger of that one of perfectly pure intellect, would not the expansive cheeks of the wives of his enemies become pale, their luster eclipsed by the waters of his gaze?
And immediately, [the truth] pervading the world was attained through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) preceded by authoritative testimony.
The ageless and auspicious supreme light spoken of shines within the heart.

O Sovereign Lady, you are the protector when the kingdom is overrun by merciless enemies; O Sovereign Lady, you are the protector when the mind is shaken by the arrows of Kāma. You are the protector of the lineage when it is seized by powerful misfortunes; and even when the cloud fails to release its water, O Sovereign Lady, you are the protector.
These two, Gaṇapati and Guha, are the Lord’s own sons, Bṛhaspati and Pāvaka incarnate;
for what reason have they been born in this land of Bharata under different guises and occupations?
O Goddess Kālī, who are filled with the sound of *kalakala*, tell me quickly what you have done.
O Mother of the Samaya, it would not be surprising if your son Rāma, having grasped your lotus feet,
were to lead you peacefully into the caves of the great mountain; for what is so wonderful in his coming here to his own place, separated from the land [of Laṅkā]?
"O Daughter of the Mountain King, you do not say from where the task for him comes."
O Mother, if the Lover of the Yoginīs speaks to the assembly of disciples this great and wondrous compendium, then what great fruit would there be for us?
Tell me, O Ambikā, when will You lead the world of living beings—who have fallen onto the wrong path—onto the right path by the power of Your immeasurable vision?
For what reason have I been born here in this most desolate place, having abandoned the shade of your lotus feet, O Queen of Māyā?
O Mother, is this some terrible and most compassionate curse of yours?
Have you perhaps been commissioned to perform some task upon the earth? || 34.10 ||
"Affection dissolves due to the power of long-distance separation"—
thus says a certain wise man; O Mother, that appears to be true,
for the Lord who was born from your own womb has gone from heaven to the earth.
Alas, alas! You act with such wrath that you have cast [him] far from the path of memory.
O Great Goddess, that stainless and heart-pleasing Vidyā which was in my mind, that wondrous and eternal Śakti which resided in my intellect,
and that great, praiseworthy fortune which existed in my speech as something most worthy of praise— alas, O Mother, all three of these have now fallen away from me upon this earth.
O Mother, I have committed a terrible sin, for while attached to virtuous deeds, I was mercilessly and repeatedly creating obstacles for men; now,
having taken this human form, I must endure its exceedingly bitter fruit.
O Māyā, wife of the Lord of Beings, be a mother to me, this one.

O Sovereign of the World, you do not come within the path of our vision; O you of great compassion, why do you not grant us a sight of yourself even in a dream? O Goddess praised by the gods, you do not remove our doubt even through your hidden grace; are you perhaps occupied with other affairs, or are you simply devoid of mercy? 34.14
The great sages proclaim your boundless majesty in Śiva; yet, as your stories are renowned, it is impossible to say that compassion is not present in your mind.
To claim that all of this is false would be an impossibility to assert.
Since you are averse to your son, what could possibly be the cause for this?
O Goddess, the sustenance of the world is no small task for you; there is never a moment when your heavy and manifold duties cease, yet that is not in vain.
Nor is your silence harsh or blameworthy, O Pārvatī.
Remember this wretched son of mine but once; that alone is sufficient for me.
This [body] does not become joyful from a shower of nectar-drops, nor is it arrogant from the production of words that steal away the intoxication of honey; yet,
this [mind] finds no satiety from attaining its final rest in the pair of Your feet.
O Blessed One, your son has been waiting for your message for a long time.
What is my duty here in this world? For what purpose have I come here to earth? And what means shall I resort to for the sake of my own power?
Whatever appears clearly within my mind amidst the darkness—O Giver of Fearlessness, please take the trouble to tell me something. (34.18)
I have no hope for supreme liberation, nor for the eightfold sovereign powers, nor for wealth consisting of a multitude of elephants, O Great Goddess;
nor do I desire the unimpeded power to create a flow of honey-dripping speech.
"O sage, from where was I born? Let that very thing be explained."
O Blessed One, I first desire sinless food for my wife, children, and guests; thereafter, O Mother, I seek unwavering devotion at your two feet.
After that, O fawn-eyed one, I wish to know the news of the world of the gods, and beyond that, to understand the cause of the enemy of the cities (Śiva) dwelling upon the earth of the sages.

O beloved wife of Śiva, you who are eager for the service of the land of Bharata; if you have compassion for me, your devoted son, who bows at your lotus feet, who is emaciated by hundreds of vows, and who offers the nectar of his head-lotus unto you.
Teach him yourself the appropriate, unclouded method.
O Mother of the worlds, even for a slight desire, he depends upon you; O Power of the Destroyer of Cities, even for a moderate desire, he depends upon you;
O Most Excellent One of abundant compassion, even for a great desire, he depends upon you.
"O Blessed One, though you have transcended all desire, even this [world] depends upon you."
O Mother, creator of the three worlds, consort of the enemy of Tripura! Out of affection for me, your humble servant, or out of maternal tenderness for one devoted to Your pair of feet,
or perhaps by the power of compassion for one intent on singing Your stainless glory— [grant me Your grace].
O Unaging One, abandon this harsh silence and reveal to me the path.
Victory to the land of Bharata, now free from sorrow! Victory to Gaṇapa, the sage whose mind is intent upon securing its welfare!
Victory to his teacher, Rāmaṇa, a mountain for the lineage of great seers!
And may their mother, the pure consort of Maheśa, be victorious.
This series of *hariṇī* verses, composed by the sage Gaṇapati, is heart-pleasing to those who know the nuances of language; it is exceedingly brilliant with the words of a virtuous poet and friend,
moving through the interior of a beautiful forest with graceful and clever sentiments.
May it delight the mind of the deer-eyed woman, the enemy of Kāma’s peace.

May the splendor of a fragment of the smile of the beloved of the Enemy of Andhaka shine for the welfare of the entire world— she who dispels blinding darkness by proclaiming the radiance of the moon, and who bestows the pure luster of her lotus-face. 35.1.
O Goddess of all, protect our family, which is diverse in its activities and full of devotion toward the assembly of the twice-born, yet lacks a refuge;
grant this boon to me, who has worshipped you for a long time.
By whom, O daughter of the mountain, your fame has been made as white as the moon.
Does it not ward off the multitude of most terrible sins, increase even that dharma which brings ultimate bliss,
and bring about what is auspicious for the servant-folk?
O Consort of Śaṅkara, [this is] the service of your feet. 35.3.

O lotus-faced one, the Goddess who dwells in the forest of lotuses attends upon that man whose heart holds your compassionate lotus feet, which are worthy of being served by those who dwell in heaven and on earth.
May he become the priest of the city of the gods in the abode of gain. || 35.4 ||

If the lotus born from the feet of the Daughter of the Mountain—whose web of qualities is sung by the entire host of sages and whose nectar of compassion dispels the fear of time—should reside within one's heart, what can Saturn do, even if it has reached the eighth house? (35.5)
O Infinite One, he who worships the garland of rays from Your feet, having offered to You the flowers of the hair on the brows of beautiful women,
shall surely cross over [saṃsāra], with his delusion extinguished.
O Mother of the entire multitude of worlds, [dispel] the darkness of grief!
O Goddess, daughter of the snowy mountain, he who remembers the lotus born from your feet— the lotus-face that robs the moon of its pride— will forget even this [world] within his heart.
Even the entire world was freed from the multitude of miseries.
O Mother of Śaktidhara, O Mistress of the house of the Fire-eyed One (Kārttikeya), O Goddess whose face conquers the full moon— this man is a virtuous soul who possesses devotion for your lotus-feet.
Like a golden-peaked mountain, it shall be a refuge for the world of the wise.
O you who hold the excellent sword that crushes the hosts of enemies in your hand,
whose garments, feet, and lips are crimson,
and whose forehead is distinguished by a fire in the guise of an eye!
Abandon all evil, O horse of the lion!

I am a soldier serving at his feet— without wages— for him who is the subject of the declarations of those who know the Vedas and their branches, and who pacifies the sorrow of the multitude of people gathered against him.
O you who possess the cool-rayed moon and the wife of Puṇya! || 35.10 ||
O Mother, whose web of virtues is sung by the enemy of Jambha, tell me— what task remains for me, whose intellect is skilled in action, who am but a servant at the feet of Your pair of lotus-lakes?
O consort of Śambhu’s lineage, you who bring about the destruction of the family of Śumbha!
If you, like a stone, do not speak, it is true that you possess no clever intellect for the affairs of state; therefore,
command us constantly as to what ought to be done according to what is appropriate.
O Queen, [I am] a servant at the lotus-feet of the world. || 35.12 ||
O Mother, having abandoned all attachment of the mind toward sons, wealth, friends, kinsmen, and wives,
this person now worships your lotus feet.
Either protect it or release it; that burden rests upon you.

O Mistress of the World, my life has been offered to the lotus-feet of you whose nails are colored by the priceless jewels set in the crowns of the hosts of gods led by Vajradhara; protect me, or do not. 35.14
O Sovereign of the World, grant my desire or do not; O Compassionate One, protect this lineage of ours or do not;
O Beloved of the Wielder of the Trident, [protect] that which is served by gods and asuras.
I shall never forsake your lotus feet, O Supreme One.
It is said that you behold the multitude of servants at your two feet; it is said that you destroy the flight of sins in times of calamity;
O mother of Gajavaktra, the wise proclaim this of you.
May this not be false, O you who are praised by the best of the inhabitants of heaven!
O you with curly, thick hair, whose feet were released by the gods led by Śakra after they had paid homage to them—
[save] this helpless one who has sought refuge [in you], submerged in calamity and rolling at your feet.
O Nandīhayasundarī, why do you not protect me? || 35.17 ||
O Mother, one who stands at your feet produces only sound;
why do you not perceive it, O Lady? Are you deaf, or is your heart captivated by the hymns of the hosts of praising gods?
O lady of the assembly of skull-bearers, may your pair of ears [be adorned].
O Mother, whose garments are like the fruit of the bimba, who performs many playful acts that rival the power of Śambara’s enemy,
you who bring delight to the one crowned by the nectar-rayed moon!
Therefore, fulfill that which you have already promised for my sake.
O you whose head is adorned by a digit of the stainless moon,
O protector of those devoted to Dharma, O compassionate one, salutations to you!
Protect this friend of the lotus-feet, O Goddess.
O daughter of the cool mountain, lead Nanda away!
O you who protect the lineage of the mountains, O banner and flag of the noble family, O you who move with the gait of a majestic elephant!
Alas, I am poor; look upon me, this wretched and pitiable one, who has sought refuge at your lotus feet.
O beloved of Rudra, O Mother, protect us; do not abandon us! || 35.21 ||
May your abiding remain forever upon the lotus-feet [of the Lord];
yet there is no peace in a heart overwhelmed by the suffering of others. O Compassionate One, let this loss of mindfulness be yours.
"Alas, mother, this great remainder of mine is a source of suffering. (35.22)
My mind was not devoid of the distinction between suffering and happiness, nor was my mind devoid of the distinction between the good and the wicked;
yet, whether it be due to my destiny or my pride, this is my lot here: that I have found an opportunity to partake in the Sangha through my mother.
Let there be the notion of duality in me; let there be a partisan stance in me;
let there be devotion to effort in me, and let there be no liberation.
I know that liberation consists in the release from the multitude of karmic afflictions inherent in my lineage.
O Great Goddess, cast your glance upon me even once.

O Mother, who makes all auspicious, whose forehead is adorned by the child-like rays of the stainless moon, you who are praised by the mouths of Viṣṇu, Indra, and Arjuna—show mercy here to this Gaṇanātha, who is noisy with the Śākvara host! 35.25

(Prakīrṇaka, in the Tūṇaka meter: May the radiance of the gentle smile of the woman who shrouds in darkness [the world]—which has always formed a bond of friendship with the spreading luster of the clusters of pearls from the necklace swaying upon the surface of her elevated breasts—dispel the dense darkness dwelling within my heart. 36.1.
She whom Purandara beheld long ago in the expanse of the sky—
whom historians call the daughter of the mountain— is that supreme consort of the Ancient God, the Mother of all.
She bathes her son; let her give her right hand.
Held in the lotus-feet by men of exclusive devotion,
and held in the lotus-hand by the one who bears the crescent of the new moon—
[the hand] possessing beautiful golden swans and lovely jeweled bracelets.
May the playful one, who protects the net of the world, purify me.
She is dearer than life to Ukṣarājavāhana;
her majesty is described by Pakṣirājavāhana and others;
and she has a son by means of Kekilokacakravartivāhana.
My vehicle is the elephant-foe, the sovereign of beasts.
Her row of teeth was like a line of young jasmine buds;
her pure cheeks were beautified by the reflections of her earrings; and she bore a pair of eyebrows that possessed the graceful charm of the staff of the Lord of Love.
Sundarī, the crest-jewel of Śubhrabhānu, is saluted.
She who protected the host of gods— assailed by the enemies of Indra, the Dākṣas, and the Yātudhānas— and who is praised by Indira and others; may she,
who shakes away the sins of her devotees with the casting of her sidelong glances, [protect us].
Pāvakākṣasundarī, who is higher than the highest, is my goal.
The daughter of the Mountain, whose lotus-face is beautiful with a gentle smile, who dances upon the stage of the mind of the Lord of the Stars (Śiva) as his crest-jewel,
and whose intellect is eternally fixed on the Buddha in his role as the nourisher of the wretched— she is the imperishable one.
It is seized by the Lord of the Gaṇas from every side at the feet of men.
The dust of the lotus-feet of the Lord, which shatters the pride of the crescent moon on the eighth day,
which serves as a swing for the mind of the Sovereign of the Three Worlds,
and which destroys the mass of sins— [that dust].
May the daughter of the mountain and the world-protector bring me prosperity.
The daughter of the Lord of the Mountain Range, with locks of hair like bees, she is like some moving statue carved from molten gold;
she is consecrated for the purpose of warding off the sorrow of people filled with devotion.
"May my sin become light through this very cool glance."
She who is a collection of auspicious names, who deludes the mind of the Enemy of Tripura, who is the charming cricket-like sound of the flower-arrowed god’s bow, the Mother of all;
she who destroys the lineage of the wicked Daityas nourished by the enemy of merit.
May the Ancient One protect my son.
Her waist was slender, her breasts resembled jars of nectar, her eyes were like those of the black antelope, and her face was as dear as the night-lotus;
she shook the steadfastness of even the golden mountain with the play of her eyebrows, which served as its bow.
Victorious is Umā, who subsists on sugarcane bows! 36.11.
The three eyes of the Lord of the Crimson Mountain bring benefit;
the cavities of the cosmic eggs sink into their crimson radiance,
and the circles of swans and cranes are made to flourish by the splendor of His smile.
May the Great Goddess make her dwelling here within my mind.

On one side, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) has blossomed from the water manifested by the radiance of His right eye; on the other side is the supreme woman, who satisfies the night-lotuses with the light of her left eye, the friend of desire.
May he of radiant fame, whose form is one, bestow auspiciousness upon us.
She is the slayer of the Daitya Śumbha, the bringer of joy to the gods,
the captivator of Śambhu’s heart, and she who dwells within the minds of the lords of sages;
she bestows desired objects and moves with the gait of a noble elephant.
May Ambikā bestow upon him the Lord of Obstacles, whose impurities have been removed.
She is a flash of fire to the forest of the lineage of those whose wives are goddesses;
she has the elephant’s enemy as her royal mount; she possesses thick tresses;
she is a certain nectar that delights the eyes of him who has Nandi as his vehicle.
May Kālikā, whose forehead is marked with the eye of wisdom, purify her son.

With a face as beautiful as a king's, walking with the gait of a royal swan, beloved by the crowns of kings, possessing a waist like that of the lord of beasts, her form shone resplendently, adorned with virtues that were truly radiant.
My mother shines resplendently upon the mountain.
Her face mocks the splendor of the lunar orb on a festival day;
she is the eternal purifier of the lineage of the Lord of Mountains;
she destroys even the scent of pride in those who wander through the night.
May she who leads the minds of all Śivas grant me auspiciousness. || 36.17 ||
The birthplace of vigor and splendor, unshakable,
with a crown bound by one who resembles the blue lotus, praised in the scriptures,
and with a bracelet fixed for the destruction of the net of the bonds of passion.
The Great Goddess Viśvapālinī is meditated upon by me. || 36.18 ||

I bow to her who is higher than the highest, by whom the cosmic egg is incessantly cooked, she who throbs within the heart-seats of all beings without exception, and whom the wise worship through the paths of breath, sight, consciousness, heat, sound, and water.
She who wears five pairs of garments, higher than the highest, worshipped by the gods;
she who is the female bee at the lotus-face of the five-faced one;
she who utterly destroys the host of internal enemies that deceive.
May she who reclines upon the couch of the departed protect my family for a long time.
The twice-born perform sacrifice to her through ritual action according to rule; those learned in the Vedas praise her as they have heard it in the Brahmanas;
and the wise contemplate her with their minds according to the instructions of their teachers.
That supreme Umā, the unborn mother of the three worlds, is victorious.
She was attended by the modest wife of Vāsudeva;
she was cherished by the strings of charming and wonderful words from Vāmadeva;
and she was gladdened by the shouts of victory for the gods, beginning with Indra.
May the daughter of the mountain-king ward off my sins.
Her face was as beautiful as the orb of the full moon,
her large, clear eyes were like the petals of a blooming lotus;
she [beheld] this son who was intent upon serving the land of merit.
May Ambikā grant the fulfillment of all desires to him who clings to her feet.
They cherish the child who is the cool-rayed moon upon their crest;
they cultivate a subtlety of mind like that of yogis;
and may they destroy the multitudes of the wicked while gathering together the assemblies of the virtuous.
And may the smiles of the women of the Enemy of Cities protect you.

May this collection of captivating *atiśakvarī* verses by the poet who serves at [His] feet—resembling a host of celestial nymphs performing a dance—be for the delight of the minds of the meritorious wives of the universal emperors of the world and for the effective warding off of their hardships. (36.25)
The Thirty-Seventh Chapter:
An Investigation into Reality (in the *Anuṣṭubh* meter). May the gentle smile of the Primordial Power (*Ādi-Śakti*) kindle our spiritual energy.
There is a doubt as to whether the subtle essence of that light is bliss. || 37.1 ||
The Knower of Wisdom is the full, existent Brahman; Maheśvarī is His knowledge—whether that be His majesty, His splendor, His power, or even His vital breath.
They declare that both the knower and the knowledge possess the nature of consciousness, just as a lamp and its light possess the form of luminosity. (37.3)
Since consciousness is a single entity, consciousness is not distinguished by [another] consciousness;
therefore, Śaṅkara rejected the view that knowledge is a quality. (37.4)
The knowledge of the knower must be its very nature (svarūpa), neither a quality (guṇa) nor an action (kriyā);
for if it were characterized by its own nature [as a separate attribute], there would be an infinite regress (anavasthiti).
The distinction between their own essential natures can be made by speech alone, not by direct experience; therefore, duality between Existence (Sat) and Power (Śakti) is merely conventional.
The sky is declared to be the object of complete knowledge of Brahman;
because of Brahman’s all-pervasiveness, it is not in reality distinct from Him. (37.7)
The wise declare that both the birth and the destruction of the sky— namely, the expansion and contraction during the two phases of creation and dissolution— are attributes of consciousness.
This supreme space, which constitutes the nature of others, is not an effect;
because it is indivisible, it is subject to no transformation, as it is not a material cause within the universe.
In the supreme space, the wisdom of the Supreme Self shone forth;
through one-pointedness, it became a profound and great light, intensified by the heat of its own fervor.
Thus, for knowledge which is the very nature of reality (dharma), there are three states—due to its purity, its objectivity, and its greatness—even without undergoing any transformation. (37.11)
Whatever entities, such as substances and qualities, appear while consciousness is manifesting,
none of them are experienced once that consciousness has ceased.
Thus, the self-luminosity of objects is not observed;
nor can their establishment occur through another without some kind of relationship [between them]. (37.13)
In both perception and recollection, the cognition is seen to take on the form of the object;
thus, the identity between the object and the cognition is directly perceived.

If the entire world were not the manifestation of the collective consciousness (samaṣṭivijñāna), its identity with the individual consciousnesses of objects (viṣayavyaṣṭivijñāna) would not be possible. || 37.15 ||
Just as in the consciousness of beings such as ourselves there is a duality of the object of meditation and the intellect,
so too in the perfect collective consciousness there is both the modification and the primordial nature.
Just as a dream is a transformation of the subtle into a gross form, so too is this waking world a transformation of the great consciousness of the Lord.
All beings are the transformation (vikṛti), while the Supreme Deity is the primordial nature (prakṛti);
of these two, the former is said to be one quarter, while the latter is proclaimed as three-quarters.

Just as even a single thought, having swallowed up [other] thoughts, becomes the intellect (*mati*), so too the Supreme Deity, having swallowed up the elements (*bhūta*), becomes [the Intellect]. 37.19.
In the creation and likewise in the withdrawal of beings, the supreme deity is the self within the self, just as the intellect is the master of volitions.
This power of the Lord, which consists of pure experience and is higher than the highest, shines forth as if divided within the bodies at the *ādhāra-cakra*. (37.21)
Then, from that [source], there arise the subtle and gross branches, like lightning, power, and wind;
therein, the first is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the subsequent one is the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
The organs of knowledge, together with the mind, constitute the first manifestation; the organs of action, together with speech, constitute the second manifestation. (37.23)
Reflecting on whether the root is action or knowledge,
the wise man who has thereby realized his own power is fit for immortality.
May these profound verses on the reality of Kālī, which are even more excellent, become like the illuminations of the intellect of Gaṇapati for the delight of the learned. 37.25.
May that gentle smile of Durgā remove all our suffering—
that smile which served as the pure plaster for the cosmic egg, fashioned from water and clay. (In the Pādākulaka meter) 38.1.
Sporting in every living being upon the earth, shining in every creature in the sky, and blazing in every deity in heaven, the fullness of consciousness manifests as if it were distinct. 38.2.

From the small lotus [of the heart] consciousness goes to the two-petaled lotus; from the two-petaled lotus to the thousand-petaled lotus; from the thousand-petaled lotus to the body; and from the body to the entire range of objects. || 38.3 ||

Like a flame of fire reaching a piece of fuel, this consciousness, having reached the entire body, becomes as if separate from it; when its power has departed, it becomes like smoke for the sake of saṃsāra. || 38.4 ||
Herein lies the experience of pleasure and pain; herein the ego-sense becomes unreal. It is here that this entire differentiated world appears when wisdom falters.
For those from whose thousand-petaled lotus descends the two-petaled lotus, and from the two-petaled lotus the heart-lotus,
wherein the Goddess descends, their inner state is eternally established.

Alternatively, having withdrawn from the body and so forth, with his intellect fixed upon the *kulakuṇḍa* situated in the support within any one of these aforementioned locations, he attains eternal steadfastness. || 38.7 ||
Śakti is in the thousand-petaled lotus, she is Lalitā in the two-petaled lotus, Vajravatī in the heart-lotus,
Bhadrā in the navel-lotus, and she who is called Bhairavī is in the mūlādhāra.
Lalitā plays, Dravati stands in her place, Aindrī shines where the knots are severed;
Bhadrā is at the closed door, and Kālī is called Bhairavī when blazing with ascetic heat.
Although Kālī and Vajreśvarī may appear as if distinct within individual bodies,
because of the unity of the principle of *ojas*, these two divisions of Śakti do not exist within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*).
Thus, although there is non-difference, there may still be duality therein due to the twofold nature of action:
she who cooks the world is Kālī, and she who burns the enemies is Aindrī.
In the aggregate and in the egg, she is the essence of the moving world; she is called pure wisdom (prajñā) and Sundarī.
In the state of the objects of the senses, having become the local manifestation (deśī), she is known as Bhuvaneśvarī. 38.12

That consciousness which, appearing as void, is dissolved in Brahmā during the dissolution and in living beings during sleep—having swallowed the entire universe—the best of poets call that the Jyeṣṭhā [the Eldest]. || 38.13 ||
Among those submerged in worldly existence, this very state manifests through the distinctions of sleep, forgetfulness, delusion, and sloth;
yet for those who practice yoga, it becomes a certain samādhi in which all conceptual constructions have been destroyed.

If the power of Indra (aindrī śakti), its strength manifest, were to split the two skull-halves, then those who possess the fourfold perspective describe it as "severed-headed" (chinnaśiraskā). || 38.15 ||
The supreme speech is Bhairavī; she is called Paśyantī when she is Tārā.
Having reached the stage of the tongue, that very one is celebrated as Mātaṅgī, the treasure-house of flavors. (38.16)
In the mass and in the egg is the power of immobilization, O Bagalā; this alone is your singular majesty.
All the rays are manifest as lotuses; O Mother of the World, such is your external majesty.
Lalita protects that steadfast person who, without relinquishing it, perceives the power of the Knower manifesting behind all volitions in every state of awakening. 38.18.

Whosoever, being steadfast, beholds whatever object they see without relinquishing the power of the seer that shines within the center of the circle of the eyes— that person is protected by the power of Indra.
Kālī protects that person who, with steady gaze, practices at every step this perpetual journey within the body that sustains the vital breath.

By means of a vision that remains in the stainless sky, freeing itself from gross transformations, or by sinking into the inner space, one attains the compassion of the Sovereign of the World. (38.21)
Having transcended all conceptual constructions and having taken recourse to the great, inner, stainless silence,
he who remains alone within as the sole one— him she, the Eldest, renders liberated.
Established in the root, the noble one who knows the secret should worship the goddess named Bhairavī-Tārā with the Udgītha chant, and that Mātaṅgī with songs of praise.
Becoming motionless through the binding of the posture and restraining the vital breath, one worships Bagalā;
perceiving the manifest splendor pervading all around, one obtains the compassion of Kamalā.

The infinite power of the Supreme Lord, which begins with a single mode and possesses many divisions, has thus been explained by the sage Gaṇapati through these *pādākulaka* verses along with the path of devotion. 38.25.
For the most part possessing a body of ether,
she pervaded this world of the moon, and for the most part, she became its pure moonlight.
May that smile of her who is beloved by all the lords of the world dispel your suffering. 39.1.
When the sky is filled, she blazes as a single lightning flash, incessantly cooking all worlds;
sometimes she flashes with splendor within a cloud.
May Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍā take away our sin. 39.2.
O Ambikā, beloved of the Lord of All, some globules are now being produced, some are being digested,
and others are attaining growth here.
When your cooking has proceeded on all sides, || 39.3 ||
O beloved of the Lord, if each single cosmic egg were as vast as your hair, it would be joined with great guides of speech and planets of immense proportions.
O Kaste, speak here of great fortune! || 39.4 ||
O Mother, the form of your Lord is subtler than the subtlest,
and yours is greater than the greatest;
O Goddess, he who knows this secret—
He is capable of explaining everything without exception.
That roar which occurs during the friction of clouds is this very sound of yours, with its profoundly deep resonance;
and that which flickers, O Queen of the World, is the manifestation of a certain wave of your radiance.
O Father, Indra’s blazing thunderbolt, the light of the thousand-rayed sun, the spreading smile of the moon, and the eye of the living soul—these are my destiny. (39.7)
I bow to that Divine Being whose splendor is distributed among the sun, lightning, moon, and fire-like eyes, yet remains hidden throughout the house of space, beyond the reach of perception.
In the waking there is consciousness; in the closing of eyes, sleep; in the dry, digestion; in the young, growth;
in the steadfast, perseverance; and in the fickle, activity.
May the Goddess remove my transgression. || 39.9 ||
The power to engage in debate belongs to the learned; the power to engage in battle belongs to the hero;
the power to enchant women belongs to the jewel among men—these are but a trifling portion of the power of the Infinite One. (39.10)
Encouraging the minds of those who practice austerity, impelling them toward great deeds,
and agitating the hearts of the wicked.
And she deludes others, leading them astray from us. || 39.11 ||
Causing the entire body to tremble by means of the pervasive power (*vyāna*) shining forth on all sides,
there is both the triumph of the conqueror and the flight of the foe.
And this entire power of the Lord belongs to one who is afraid. || 39.12 ||
Displaying her single true nature in manifold ways through various combinations to people,
she presents her own all-pervading self to those who see correctly.
She is indeed the primordial illusion, the consort of Maheśa.
Whoever should take refuge in you—
the bearer of the burden of sovereignty over the three worlds— whether by meditation, by mantra, or by hymns of praise, shall attain the company of all.
That virtuous man was beloved within the inner apartments of the harem. || 39.14 ||
O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, you [reside] in that fortunate man who, having kindled the fire at the base and caused the moon in his head to flow, satiates you.
As you appear, do you not bestow [something]? 39.15.
O Mother, the yogi who worships you in the form of the Moon within the thousand-petaled lotus—
his inner torment attains peace.
What need is there to mention the insignificant external world? || 39.16 ||
He who has entered within the small space by means of the staff,
or by vital breath, speech, splendor, or intellect—
this very person attains the peerless city.
Where you, O Sovereign, are with Citralīlā. || 39.17 ||
O Rudrāṇī, whose mass of hair is like dense clouds, that self-controlled man who worships the mantra taught in the Tantra for the guidance of the universe— [attains success].
Freed from the bonds, he conquers everything without exception.
Padmāsana, Dvādaśavarṇaśānti, Dambholipāṇi, Bhuvanādhinātha, Gīrvāṇamārga, Bhṛgu, and Abjayoni; at the end as well as at the beginning, Halāṃvirāja likewise [appears]. 39.19.
The slayer of Jambha, joined with Anala, Śānti, and Candra, is the *ūṣman* born in the region of the throat;
it is the *ūṣman* phoneme produced from the site of the teeth.
The Lord of Speech, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, and Modesty.
This Vidyā, enriched with fifteen syllables,
was directly taught by the great sage Maunaguru; it is the most secret of secrets, to be attained only through meritorious deeds.
They are most excellent even when praised by the Supreme Lord.
In bodies she is called Kuṇḍalinī; among the elements, lightning; and in the worlds, the cloud.
Among the deities, she is indeed the goddess Bhavānī, whose feet are cherished by the heads of the celestial maidens.
If one gazes at the vital breath (prāṇa) within the immovable space between the eyes, perceiving it as the form of the syllable *manu*,
and thus serves the Sustainer of all;
For the wise man, the attainment of all that is desired is held within the palm of his hand.
For one who, endowed with devotion, recites these mantras— whether consisting of a single syllable or fifteen syllables— which are the preeminent vidyās of the power of the Lord of All, for him...
The vital breath is under control; it is the source of incomparable accomplishment.
May these pure verses in the Indravajrā meter, sung with the melting flow of devotion by one who is a servant at the feet of the sages, bring forth supreme joy.
Of the beloved of the Lord of Śvetācala. || 39.25 ||

May the gentle smile of the beautiful-eyed lady of the lineage of the Mind-born’s command pacify our sin, subdue our suffering, remove our delusion, clarify our awakening, and expand our power— this song of destiny! (In the *pādākulaka* meter) 40.1.
Moist with compassion, having brought the king of the gods under the sway of her glance by her power, and worthy of worship by all women—may that woman remove my misfortune entirely. 40.2
In the pure Brahman, joy is the divine; therein, the desire to create is the divine;
in creating objects, vision is the divine; and in sustaining them, majesty is the divine. (40.3)
In every transformation, the primordial nature is destiny; in every object, existence is destiny.
In every perception, valid cognition is destiny; in every meditation, steadfastness is destiny. (40.4)
In every manifestation, Māyā is the divine power; in every movement, Śakti is the divine power;
in every splendor, Lakṣmī is the divine power; and in every sound, Vāṇī is the divine power. || 40.5 ||
In every heart dwells the living deity; in every head dwells the meditating deity;
in every eye dwells the shining deity; at every root dwells the scorching deity.
Divine light spreads throughout the sky on all sides; divine light grows upon the world of earth;
divine light blazes within the orb of the sun; divine light pours down from the orb of the moon.

Hearing again and again the divine name that is to be known; reciting again and again the divine name that is to be attained; remembering again and again the divine name that is to be held fast; praising again and again the divine name that is to be lauded. (40.8)
In the Vedas, the deity is to be grasped by students; for householders, the deity is to be gratified in the fire;
for ascetics, the deity is nourished upon the head; and for renunciants, the deity remains as the residual essence within the heart.
The Divine is to be worshipped with prostrations and flowers by the poet; the Divine is to be propitiated through verse by the scholar;
the Divine is to be meditated upon with the mind by the sage; and the Divine is to be purified within one's own self by the ascetic.
The Divine bestows speech upon those who praise; the Divine clarifies the mind of those who remember;
the Divine expands the power of those who recite prayers; the Divine subdues the evil of those who bow down. 40.11.
The divine power that disciplines speech resides in fire; the divine power that disciplines the vital breaths resides in lightning;
the divine power that disciplines desires resides in the moon; and the divine power that disciplines the intellects resides in the sun.
Dwelling in the heart, fate grasps; dwelling in the bladder, fate releases;
dwelling in the throat, fate speaks; dwelling in the belly, fate digests.
The deity residing within the body, the deity manifesting as the five vital breaths; the deity that partakes of all food, and the deity that is satisfied by the utterance of "svāhā. (40.14)
Bearing a divine woman’s attire, radiant with a bright and gentle smile, divine; with hair that dispels the clouds, divine; the very abode of graceful charm, divine. (40.15)
The divine one has a face like the cool-rayed moon; the divine one has teeth resembling drops of luster;
the divine one is an abode of the nectar of beauty; the divine one intoxicates the eyes of the enemy of Smara (Śiva). 40.16.
Fate has a forehead with waves of beauty; fate has eyes with waves of wisdom;
fate has a lower lip with waves of splendor; fate has a face with waves of joy.

The Lord whose eyes are overflowing with compassion; the Lord whose ears possess the luster of the syllable Śrī; the Lord whose limbs are as tender as a flower; the Lord who is the vessel for the majesty of the poets' speech. 40.18.
On the Himavat mountain, the divine is manifest; on the peak of the white mountain, the divine sports.
The divine is sung by Tumburu and Nārada; the divine is meditated upon by gods, sages, and perfected beings.
In one place, destiny is charming with hundreds of pleasures; in another place, destiny is exceedingly fierce.
Destiny assumes a form that follows the mind of the devotee; destiny possesses a power that follows the mind of the yogi.
For those who praise the divine, it is sweet in their conduct; for those who bow at the divine feet, it is sweet in their feet.
For Śambhu, the divine is sweet in his lower lip; but for me, the divine is sweet in my breast.
Fate is that which bears the burden of the world upon its arms; fate is that which holds the essence of prosperity at its feet;
fate is that which caresses the heroes among the gods; fate is that which protects the courageous and virtuous.

Victorious is that Divinity, praised by the three worlds, who is celebrated in the Vedas as Śiva—the Divinity whose nature is the power of consciousness (cicchakti) in the microcosm (adhyātma), and who is the Divinity in the form of lightning in the macrocosm (adhibhūta). 40.23.
This Vāsiṣṭha, a disciple of the great seer Ramaṇa and the middle son of Narasiṃha, approaches the feet of Gaṇapati, the mother of the Maruts, for refuge. (40.24)

Victorious is Gaurī, the supreme power of the Lord of the three worlds, the mother of all! Victorious is this hymn of praise to her, composed by Gaṇapati, ending in the Pādākulaka meter. 40.25. 1000. And the tenth century is completed.
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Vāsiṣṭha, disciple of the blessed great seer Ramaṇa and son of Narasiṃha.
The *Umāsahasra*, the work of Gaṇapati, is completed.
